title: Booking a holiday cottage
setting: Một khách hàng gọi điện đến công ty cho thuê nhà nghỉ Fernhill để đặt một căn nhà cho kỳ nghỉ gia đình vào tháng Bảy.
lines: Good morning, Fernhill Holiday Cottages. Sarah speaking. How can I help you?
Oh, hi. I'm ringing about booking one of your cottages in July. For a week, or maybe a little less.
Lovely. Let me just open a booking form. Could I take your name first?
Could you spell the surname for me, please?
Thank you, Mr Whitcombe. And is this your first time staying with us?
It is. A friend of mine stayed with you last year and said it was really peaceful.
That's nice to hear. So, which cottage were you interested in?
Well, my friend stayed in Willow Cottage, so I was hoping for that one.
I'm afraid Willow Cottage is fully booked for the whole of July. But we do have Heron Cottage, which is very similar. It's right next to the stream.
Heron Cottage. Does it have two bedrooms?
Yes, one double and one twin, so it sleeps four people.
That's perfect. It'll be me, my wife and our two kids. Let's go with Heron, then.
Great. And what date would you like to arrive?
We were thinking of Saturday the twelfth of July.
Let me check. Hmm, Heron is taken until the thirteenth, I'm afraid. The earliest you could arrive is Monday the fourteenth.
Oh, right. Well, the fourteenth is fine. We're quite flexible.
So, arriving on the fourteenth. And how long would you like to stay?
We originally wanted a whole week, but with the later start, let's say five nights.
Five nights, so you'd leave on the morning of the nineteenth.
That works. Can I ask about the price?
Of course. In July, Heron Cottage is 110 pounds a night.
Oh, that's a bit more than I expected, to be honest.
Well, if you book more than two weeks in advance, there's a discount, which brings it down to 95 pounds a night.
That's much better. We'll definitely book today, then.
Is there anything else you'd like to add to your booking? We offer a breakfast basket, and some guests like to hire bicycles.
We'll bring our own food, I think, but the bicycles sound like fun. The kids would love that.
I'll add bicycles, then. They're actually free for guests, but you do need to reserve them.
Even better. Oh, and one more thing. We have a dog. Is that a problem?
Not at all. Dogs are welcome in Heron Cottage. There's a charge of 15 pounds to cover the extra cleaning.
No, it's just once for the whole stay.
Fair enough. And where do we park when we arrive?
There's no parking on the lane, because it's very narrow. You'll need to use the courtyard behind the cottage. There's room for two cars.
The courtyard, OK. And how do we get the keys?

Normally guests collect them from the village shop, but the shop closes at lunchtime on Mondays. So, as you're arriving on a Monday, you'll need to pick them up from the post office instead. It's open until six.
Right, the post office. I'll make a note of that.
Just one last question. We like to know how our guests heard about us. Was it only through your friend?
Partly, but I'd also seen your advert in a walking magazine. I can't remember which one, though.
That's fine, I'll just put walking magazine. Now, shall I take the deposit?

title: Open day at Riverside City Farm
setting: Một điều phối viên giới thiệu với khách tham quan về lịch sử, nội quy và các hoạt động trong ngày hội mở cửa của trang trại thành phố Riverside.
lines: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Riverside City Farm's open day. My name's Megan, and I'm one of the farm coordinators.
Before you head off to explore, I'd like to tell you a little about the farm and about what's going on today.

A lot of people assume the farm was started by the local council. In fact, the council only gave us the land. The idea came from a group of parents who wanted their children to see where food comes from.
That was back in 1998, when this whole area was an empty car park. Hard to imagine now, isn't it?
At first, everything was done by volunteers, and the parents ran the place on almost no money at all. These days we have six paid staff, and people often ask how we pay for it all.
Well, we do receive some money from school visits, and of course the donations box by the gate helps a great deal.
But by far the biggest share of our income now comes from selling what we grow and produce here, mainly vegetables, eggs and honey, at our weekly market on Saturdays.
Now, a few rules. You're very welcome to take photographs of the animals, and all the paths are suitable for pushchairs and wheelchairs.
What we do ask is that you don't give the animals any food yourselves, even if they look hungry. Many of them are on special diets, and the wrong food can make them quite ill.

One more practical thing. Those of you who've been here before will notice that the café has moved. It used to be next to the main gate, but it's now in the old dairy building, which has much more space.
The prices haven't changed, I'm pleased to say, and it still closes at four o'clock, so do get your tea and cake before then.
So, what's happening today? Let me take you round the farm.

Starting with the Goat Barn, just on your left. The goats had their breakfast early this morning, but at eleven the staff will be giving them their lunch, and children are welcome to help. Adults can join in too, if you like.
Next, the Orchard. We grow about forty varieties of apple there. Unfortunately the fruit won't be ready to pick until September.
However, one of our volunteers, Colin, will be leading a walk through the trees at two o'clock, explaining how we look after them through the year.
Moving on to the Pond. If you have younger children, bring them along at half past twelve.

We'll be sitting on the benches by the water, and one of our team will read a story about a family of ducks. It's very popular, so come early. And please keep a close eye on small children near the water.
In the Workshop, we'd planned a craft session for today, but sadly the tutor is unwell.
Instead, our blacksmith will be showing how he makes hooks and gate latches. You can't have a go yourselves, I'm afraid, as it's far too dangerous, but it's fascinating to watch.
The Greenhouse is where we raise all our seedlings. Today there'll be tables of tomato, pepper and herb plants on sale, all grown here, at very reasonable prices.
Finally, the Meadow. In the big white tent there, you can learn willow weaving and make a small basket or a bird feeder to take home.
All the materials are provided, and it's suitable for anyone over the age of eight.
Right, I think that's everything. Enjoy your day, and if you have any questions, just look for someone in a green T-shirt.

title: A survey on cycling to campus
setting: Hai sinh viên trao đổi với giảng viên hướng dẫn về kết quả khảo sát lý do sinh viên đạp xe (hoặc không) đến trường và cách viết báo cáo.
lines: Come in, Lucy, Tom. So, you wanted to talk about your cycling project before you write it up.
Yes, thanks for seeing us, Dr Patel. We've collected all the data now, so we just wanted to check a few things.
Good. Remind me first why you chose cycling. It's not the most obvious topic for a sociology project.
Well, I cycle in every day, so I was interested, but Lucy doesn't even own a bike.
That's true. The real reason was that we read in the student newspaper that the university is reviewing its transport policy next year. We thought our findings might actually be useful to them.
That's a good motivation. Now, how did the questionnaire go?
Better than we expected in terms of numbers. We got 212 responses, which is more than we needed.
And most people said it only took about five minutes to complete, so that wasn't an issue either.
The problem was question six. We asked how far people lived from campus, but we didn't say whether we meant miles or kilometres. So some of the answers are impossible to compare.
Ah. That kind of thing happens to everyone. You'll just need to mention it as a limitation.
We will. What really surprised us was the reasons people gave for not cycling. We expected the weather to come top, because it rains so much here.
But hardly anyone mentioned it. Only about four per cent.
Safety was the biggest concern, which we'd more or less predicted, and after that, not having anywhere to leave a bike.
Interesting. And I see from your plan that you also want to interview some local bike shop owners.
Yes, we thought they'd know a lot about who cycles and why.
They might, but your research question is about students' choices. Shop owners can't really tell you what students think. I'd drop that idea and focus on the students themselves.
OK, that makes sense. We were a bit worried about the time it would take anyway.
Now, you also asked people what changes would encourage them to cycle. What came out on top?
Well, quite a few people wanted more cycle lanes, but the campus already has quite a lot, so I think some people just don't know about them.
The clear winner was secure storage. People are really worried about bikes being stolen, and the racks we have now are just outside, with no cameras.
And second, a lot of people said they'd cycle if there were proper changing rooms with showers, so they didn't arrive at lectures all hot and sweaty.
A few mentioned a repair workshop, and one or two said bikes are too expensive, but those were much smaller numbers.
So storage and changing facilities. That gives you a clear focus for your recommendations.
We were thinking of suggesting cameras on the existing racks as a first step, because that would be quite cheap.
Good, practical ideas tend to impress readers. Right, let's talk about the structure of the report. You've got a background section first.
Yes, I was wondering whether we even need it. Maybe we could just leave it out.
No, you do need some context, but at the moment it's nearly two pages. Cut it down to half a page at most.
Fine. What about the questionnaire itself? We put the full list of questions in the methods section.
It's useful for the reader to see it, but it interrupts the flow. Put it at the end of the report, in an appendix, and just summarise it in the methods.
The charts are clear, but you've only shown the overall figures. I'd like to see the results broken down by year group and by gender, so there's more to discuss.
That's easy enough. We have all that data.
And finally, the recommendations. We weren't sure if they were too short.
No, actually, they're fine. They're specific and they follow from your data. I wouldn't change anything there.
Great. Thanks, Dr Patel, that's really helpful.

title: The history of ice houses
setting: Bài giảng về lịch sử các nhà chứa băng (ice house): cách xây dựng, cách bảo quản băng, công dụng và lý do chúng biến mất.
lines: Good afternoon. In today's lecture in our series on the history of everyday technology, I'm going to talk about ice houses.
Before refrigerators, how did people keep things cold? For centuries, the answer was to collect natural ice in winter and store it, somehow, so that it lasted through the summer.

An ice house, then, is simply a building designed to keep ice frozen for as long as possible. Most were built completely or partly underground, because the temperature of the earth stays fairly constant throughout the year.
Some of the most impressive early examples come from ancient Persia, in what is now Iran. These structures were called yakhchals, and some of them are still standing today.
What made them so effective was the material of the walls. The builders used a special mortar that was highly resistant to heat.
It contained sand, clay, egg whites, lime and goat hair, and also ash, which helped to make the walls almost completely waterproof.

Above ground, a yakhchal had a tall dome shape. This was not just for decoration. Warm air rose to the top of the dome and escaped through a small opening, while the coldest air sank down to the storage pit below.

Let's move to Europe. Ice houses appeared in Italy and France quite early, but in Britain they only became common in the seventeenth century, when wealthy landowners began building them on their country estates.
By the nineteenth century, there were thousands of them across the country, and many survive today.
So where did the ice come from? Some people assume it was cut from rivers, but moving water rarely freezes thick enough.
In fact, estate workers usually broke ice from the surface of lakes, and many estates even dug artificial ones especially for this purpose.
This work was done in the coldest weeks of January and February, and it was hard and dangerous. Workers stood on the frozen surface with hammers and poles, and accidents were common.

The ice was then broken into small pieces and packed tightly into the pit. This was important, because small pieces freeze together into one solid mass, which melts much more slowly than separate blocks.
Insulation was the next challenge. Between the layers of ice, workers spread straw.
Sawdust was sometimes used in later periods, but straw was cheaper and easier to find on a farm estate, so it was the standard choice.

Of course, some melting was unavoidable, and water lying in the bottom of the pit would speed up the process. So the floor of an ice house always sloped towards a drain, which carried the meltwater away.
What was the ice actually used for? Mainly for preserving food, such as fish, meat and dairy products.
It was also used for making ice cream and cold drinks for parties, which were a way of showing off one's wealth.
But ice had medical uses as well. Doctors used it to bring down a fever, and to reduce swelling after injuries.
In the nineteenth century, ice became a business. As cities grew, demand far exceeded what local lakes could provide.
At first, ice was shipped across the Atlantic from North America, but this was expensive. Later, most of the ice sold in London came from Norway, which was much closer and had plenty of frozen lakes.
Large commercial ice wells were dug in London to store these imports. One of them, near King's Cross, is now part of a museum, and visitors can still look down into it.
So why did ice houses disappear? The answer, of course, is mechanical refrigeration.
By the early twentieth century, ice could be manufactured in factories all year round, and later, refrigerators in people's homes made stored natural ice unnecessary.

It's worth remembering, though, that the change was gradual. In country areas, some estates went on filling their ice houses every winter until well into the nineteen-thirties, simply because it cost them almost nothing.
Today, many old ice houses survive in parks and gardens, and some have found new uses. A number of them have become homes for bats, which like the cool, dark and stable conditions.
Next week, we'll look at another everyday technology that we now take for granted: the history of street lighting.

title: Enquiring about evening courses
setting: Một người mới chuyển đến gọi điện cho trung tâm giáo dục người lớn Larchfield để hỏi về ba khóa học và đăng ký một khóa.
lines: Good afternoon, Larchfield Adult Education Centre. How can I help?
Hi there. I've just moved to the area, and I'm interested in some of your courses. I picked up a leaflet, but it's from last year, so I wanted to check the details.
Of course. Which courses are you looking at?
Three, actually. I haven't quite decided yet. The first one is digital photography.
Right. That used to run on Monday evenings, but this term it's on Tuesdays, from seven till nine.
Tuesday, OK. And how much does it cost? The leaflet says 125 pounds.
That was last year's price. It's gone up to 140 pounds now, I'm afraid, for ten weeks.
That's still reasonable. Who teaches it?
A professional photographer called Helen Grayson. That's G-R-A-Y-S-O-N.
Grayson. Thanks. Do I need my own camera?
You can use a phone camera to begin with, actually. But you'll need to bring a laptop each week, because a lot of the course is about editing your photos.
OK, I've got a laptop, so that's fine. The second one I was looking at is Italian for beginners.
That's on Wednesdays, also in the evening. It's 95 pounds for the term, and that includes a dictionary, which you get to keep. The textbook you'll need to buy separately.
And is it held in the main building?
Not this term. Our classrooms are being decorated, so the Italian class meets in the library on Park Street. It's just across the road from us.
The library. Got it. And the last one is furniture restoration.
Ah, that's very popular. It isn't in the evening, though. It's on Saturday, from ten until one, in our workshop.
Saturday mornings would actually suit me better. Is there anything I need to bring for that one?
All the tools are provided, but you're asked to bring a small piece of furniture to work on, like a chair or a little table. And wear old clothes.
180 pounds, but that includes all the materials, like paint and varnish.
That sounds good value. When do the courses actually start?
All three begin in the week of the twenty-second of September, and they run until early December, with a one-week break at the end of October.
And is there parking at the centre? I'll be driving, at least at first.
There's a small car park behind the main building, but it fills up quickly in the evenings. Most people use the public car park on Mill Lane, which is free after six.
OK, that's useful to know. I think I'll sign up for the photography course now, and maybe add the others later.
Lovely. I'll just take a few details. Can I have your full name?
It's 31 Ashgrove Road. Ashgrove is A-S-H-G-R-O-V-E.
31 Ashgrove Road. Lovely. And how would you prefer us to contact you about the course? We can send an email or a text.
Emails tend to get lost in my inbox, so a text would be better.
No problem. I'll send you a text to confirm your place this afternoon, and you can pay online.
Great. Thanks so much for your help.

title: The Harbour Lights Festival
setting: Người dẫn chương trình radio địa phương giới thiệu lễ hội Harbour Lights ở thị trấn ven biển Port Ellery: lịch sử, vé, thay đổi năm nay và lịch các sự kiện.
lines: Good morning, and you're listening to Coast FM. I'm Jack Morrison.
This morning I'm going to tell you everything you need to know about this year's Harbour Lights Festival, which starts in Port Ellery next Friday and runs for three days.
For anyone who's new to the area, the festival began twenty-five years ago as a small fishing competition for local families.
Over time it grew to include music and food, and these days it's probably best known for the lantern parade along the harbour on the final night.
Now, a question we get asked every year is how much it costs. Entry to the festival area is free, as always, and that includes the lantern parade and all the activities on the beach.
The only event you need a ticket for is the concert on Saturday night, and those are 25 dollars from the visitor centre.
Last year, more than thirty thousand people came along, which caused some real headaches.

It wasn't the weather, which was perfect all weekend, and there were plenty of food stalls. The problem was that the roads into town were completely blocked, and some visitors spent over an hour trying to find a parking space.
So this year the organisers have made some changes. First, there'll be free shuttle buses running every fifteen minutes from the sports ground on the edge of town.
You can park there for nothing, and the bus will drop you right by the harbour.
The second big change is that, for the first time, there'll be a children's zone on the beach, with games, face painting and a small stage for younger performers.
Some of you have asked whether the fireworks are coming back. I'm afraid they're not. The council decided last year that they upset the local wildlife, especially the seabirds.
The craft market is back again, as usual, in the town square, and it'll be open all three days.
Right, let me run through the main events and when they're on, because a few things have moved around.
The fishing competition, where it all began, used to be held on the Sunday. This year it's been moved to Saturday morning, starting at six. So set your alarms.
On Friday afternoon, after school finishes, there's sandcastle building on the main beach for families. There are prizes for the most creative design, not just the biggest.
The cooking competition has been running for ten years now. The early rounds take place on Saturday, but the final, which is the part really worth watching, is on Sunday at noon.
The dragon boat race was supposed to be on Saturday afternoon, but because of the tides, the organisers have moved it to Friday evening, at around six.
And of course, the festival ends with the lantern parade on Sunday evening, starting at eight from the lighthouse. If you'd like to carry a lantern, you can make one at the craft market beforehand.
Before I go, a quick word about volunteers. The festival simply couldn't happen without them, and this year the organisers still need around sixty more people.

Jobs include giving out maps, helping at the shuttle bus stops and collecting rubbish on the beach. You only need to give four hours of your time, and every volunteer gets a free festival T-shirt and a meal voucher.
If you're interested, you can sign up at the visitor centre on Beach Road, or call in to the radio station this week and we'll pass your name on.

title: Food waste in the university canteen
setting: Hai sinh viên thảo luận với giảng viên về bài thuyết trình nghiên cứu lãng phí thực phẩm ở căng tin trường: kết quả, cách mở đầu, phân công và khuyến nghị.
lines: Hello, Hannah, Raj. Come and sit down. So, your presentation on food waste is next Thursday. How's it coming along?
Pretty well, I think. We've finished the research, and now we're working on the slides.
We wanted to run a few things past you first, especially the findings.
Of course. Remind me how you collected your data.
We worked with the main canteen for two weeks. Every evening, the kitchen staff measured the weight of all the food that was thrown away, and we recorded it in a spreadsheet.
We also kept a note of what type of food it was, so we could look for patterns.
The biggest category by far was bread. Nearly a third of the total waste. A lot of it was from the free rolls they put out with the soup.
We'd assumed it would be cooked vegetables, but they actually came second.
That's quite striking. Did the canteen manager have an explanation?
She said they put the rolls out in big baskets, and students take two or three without thinking, then leave most of them on the plate.

Another thing we noticed was that waste was much higher on Fridays. We think that's because lots of students go home for the weekend, so fewer people eat in the canteen, but the kitchen still prepares the same amount.
So part of the problem is planning rather than students' behaviour.
We also did a short survey. We asked students why they left food. We thought they'd complain about the taste, but only a few did. The most common answer was that the portions were too big.
Now, have you decided how to start the presentation? First impressions really matter.
I wanted to open with a list of statistics about food waste around the world, to show how serious it is.
And I thought we could start with a photo. We took a picture of one day's waste, all piled up on a table. It's quite shocking.
I'd go with the photo. Statistics are important, but if you start with too many numbers, the audience will switch off. The image will grab their attention, and then you can bring in the figures.
How are you dividing up the work?
We thought Raj would present the data and I'd do the recommendations.
Although actually, I'm more comfortable talking about solutions, and Hannah made all the charts, so maybe it makes more sense the other way round.
That's true. OK, let's swap, then.
Good. And how long is it at the moment?
About twenty-five minutes in total, if we include everything.
That's too long. The limit is twenty minutes, and that includes five minutes for questions at the end. So you've really only got fifteen minutes of talking.
Right. We'll have to cut quite a lot, then.
One more thing. Are you planning to include the canteen manager's comments?
We have a recording of the interview, but the sound quality isn't great. There's a lot of kitchen noise.
Then don't play it. Choose one or two good sentences and put a short quotation on a slide instead.
Finally, the recommendations. How many have you got?
We had five ideas originally. We've already dropped charging for bread rolls, because the manager said students would complain.
We're definitely keeping smaller portions, with the option of asking for more. That came straight from the survey.
Donating leftovers to a local charity was a nice idea, but there are hygiene rules that make it really difficult, so we've taken that out as well.
And reducing the number of dishes on the menu. The manager said that would be very unpopular, so that's gone too.
But adjusting how much the kitchen cooks on Fridays is simple and cheap, so that's our second one.
Two clear, practical recommendations. That's much better than five vague ones. Well done, both of you.

title: Bioluminescence in the ocean
setting: Bài giảng sinh học biển về hiện tượng phát quang sinh học: cơ chế, màu sắc, chức năng đối với động vật và ứng dụng cho con người.
lines: Good morning, everyone. Today we're turning to one of the most remarkable phenomena in marine biology: bioluminescence, which is simply the production of light by living organisms.
It's far more common than most people realise. Scientists now estimate that around three quarters of the animals living in the open ocean are able to produce light.
That figure comes from years of observations made with cameras on remotely operated vehicles, which can film animals at depths no diver could ever reach.
On land, by contrast, it's quite rare. Fireflies are the best-known example, along with a few types of fungi.
So how does it work? In most cases, the light is produced by a chemical reaction. A molecule called luciferin reacts with oxygen, and this reaction is controlled by an enzyme.
The energy is released almost entirely as light rather than heat, which is why bioluminescence is sometimes described as cold light.
Interestingly, not all animals make these chemicals themselves. Some get luciferin from their diet, by eating smaller glowing organisms.
Others, like the bobtail squid, host colonies of bacteria that glow on their behalf. In return, the squid gives the bacteria food and a safe place to live.
Now, if you've ever seen photographs of glowing sea creatures, you'll have noticed that most of the light is blue. That's because blue light travels furthest through seawater.
Red light, on the other hand, is absorbed very quickly, which is why most deep-sea animals can't see red at all.
So why do animals produce light? There are several functions. The first is defence.
Some deep-sea shrimps, when they're attacked, release a cloud of glowing liquid, rather like a squid releasing ink. This confuses the predator while the shrimp escapes into the darkness.
The second function is hunting. The anglerfish is the classic example. It has a long spine on its head with a glowing tip, which it uses like a fishing rod to attract smaller fish close to its mouth.
A third function is camouflage, and this one is rather clever. Many animals in the middle depths produce light on their undersides.
When a predator looks up from below, the animal's glow matches the faint sunlight coming from above, so its shadow disappears.
Biologists call this counter-illumination. Some animals can even adjust the brightness of their glow as they move up and down, to match the changing light levels around them.
And finally, there's communication. Some species use flashing patterns to find a mate, much as fireflies do on land.
In certain small fish, males and females produce slightly different patterns of flashes, so that individuals can recognise members of their own species in the dark.
Bioluminescence has also had practical value for humans. The most important example came from a jellyfish that produces a green fluorescent protein.

Scientists learned to attach this protein to other genes, so that they can see exactly where and when those genes are active inside living cells. The researchers who developed this were awarded a Nobel Prize in 2008.
There have also been some less successful ideas. A few years ago, a project proposed replacing street lights with glowing trees, created by adding bioluminescent genes to plants.

Some people raised concerns about releasing modified plants, but that isn't what ended the project. The real problem was that the light produced was far too weak to be useful, and the idea was eventually abandoned.

Bioluminescence is also helping us to monitor the environment. Certain glowing bacteria become dimmer when they're exposed to toxic chemicals, so they can be used to test water quality quickly and cheaply.
This is much faster than traditional laboratory tests, which can take several days to give a result.
To finish, I want to stress how much we still don't know. Most of the deep ocean has never been explored, and almost every expedition discovers new light-producing species.
Researchers now believe that bioluminescence has evolved independently many dozens of times in different groups of animals.
When something evolves again and again like that, it tells us that producing light must give animals a very strong advantage for survival.
In our next session, we'll look at the other side of the story: how deep-sea animals detect light.

title: Joining a badminton club
setting: Một người mới chuyển đến gọi điện cho câu lạc bộ cầu lông để đăng ký làm hội viên.
lines: Good evening, Riverside Badminton Club, Helen speaking. How can I help?
Oh, hi. I'm ringing because I'd like to join the club. I've just moved to the area, and I saw on a poster that you take new members in the autumn.
We do, yes. I can take a few details now, if that's convenient, and then I'll tell you about the sessions and the fees.
Right. Could I have your name first, please?
Could you spell the surname for me?
Thank you. And what's your address, Daniel?
I'm at 14 Thornbury Road. That's T-H-O-R-N-B-U-R-Y.
Lovely, I know it. That's just behind the leisure centre, isn't it?
That's right, it's about five minutes' walk from there.
And may I ask what you do for a living? We only ask because some of our sessions take place during the day.
I used to be a pharmacist, actually, but I retrained a couple of years ago. Now I'm a nurse at the city hospital, so I work shifts.
Oh, interesting. Now, how would you describe your level of play? We have beginner, intermediate and advanced groups.
Well, I played in a league back home in Perth, so I was going to say advanced.
But to be honest, I haven't played for about three years. Put me down as intermediate for now.
That's sensible. You can always move up once the coaches have seen you play.
The intermediate group meets twice a week, on Tuesday evenings and on Thursday evenings. Do you have a preference?
Tuesday would suit me best, I think.
Ah, I'm afraid the Tuesday group is completely full at the moment. There's a waiting list, though.
Oh, right. Well, in that case, Thursday is fine. My shifts usually finish early on Thursdays anyway.
I'll put you down for Thursday evenings, then. Now, membership. We have three types. Full membership lets you use the courts at any time.
That's 210 pounds a year. Then there's off-peak membership, which covers weekday evenings after eight o'clock, and weekends.
Hmm. The group sessions start at eight, don't they?
The Thursday group starts at a quarter past eight, so off-peak would cover it.
Then I'll go for off-peak. What does that cost?
It's 165 pounds a year. The third option is pay as you play, but that works out more expensive if you come every week.
No, off-peak sounds right for me.
Do you have your own racket?
Yes, I brought two with me when I moved.
Good. The only other thing you need is a pair of indoor shoes. Running shoes with black soles leave marks on the floor, so we don't allow them.
OK, indoor shoes. I'll have to buy some.
There's a sports shop on the high street that sells them quite cheaply. Now, just for our records, how did you hear about the club? Was it through our website?
No, I haven't looked at the website yet. I saw your poster on the noticeboard at the library.
Oh, that's nice to know someone reads them! When you arrive for your first session, ask for our head coach, Marcus Ferreira.
Got it. And where's the best place to park?
The car park at the front is often full, so use the one behind the bakery on Mill Lane. It's free after six.
Behind the bakery. Brilliant. Thanks so much, Helen.
You're welcome, Daniel. See you on Thursday.

title: A tour of a textile museum
setting: Hướng dẫn viên giới thiệu với khách tham quan về một bảo tàng dệt may đặt trong một nhà máy cũ.
lines: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Kingsbridge Textile Museum. My name's Fiona, and I'll be your guide for the next hour or so.
Before we set off, a few practical points. This building was a working mill until 1968, so some of the floors are uneven. Please watch your step, especially on the stairs.
You're welcome to take photographs anywhere in the museum. The only thing I'd ask is that you switch off your flash in the dyeing room.
That's not because the room is dark, although it is a little gloomy. It's because the old fabric samples on display there fade very easily in bright light.
Now, a little history. The mill was built in 1821 by a local family, the Ashworths. A lot of visitors assume it always made cotton, but for its first fifty years it actually produced wool.
You'll sometimes read that the switch happened because the wool trade collapsed. That isn't really true, as wool sales in the region stayed fairly steady.
What changed things was the railway. Once it reached the town in the 1870s, it became far cheaper to bring raw cotton up from the port, and the Ashworths took advantage of that.
One more thing before we start. Some of you may have heard that we were planning to open a rooftop café this year. Sadly, that's been delayed until next spring.
We're also still raising money for an audio guide. What we have launched this year is a trail for children, with a stamp to collect in every room. The children's booklets are at the front desk.
Right, let's look at the map on your leaflet so you know what's where. We'll begin downstairs in the Engine House.
The steam engine there is the heart of the building. We only run it on the first Sunday of each month, so you won't see it moving today, I'm afraid.
But there's a short film playing on a loop in the corner. It shows how our volunteers spent ten years restoring the engine and the rest of the mill, and it's well worth ten minutes.
Next door is the Weaving Hall, where you'll find twenty of the original looms. One of them is switched on every day, at eleven and again at three. Be warned, the noise is incredible.

Upstairs is the Dyeing Room. Along the walls there are jars of the plants that were used to make dyes. Please feel free to pick the jars up and smell them, and you can touch the pieces of dyed wool too.
We did run dyeing workshops in that room for a while, but they were too messy, so we stopped.

Across the yard are the Workers' Cottages, furnished as they would have been in the 1890s. If you sit on the bench by the fireplace and press the button, you'll hear interviews recorded in the 1970s with people who worked here as teenagers.
And finally, on the top floor, there's the Archive Room. It holds the mill's account books, but that's not the main reason to go up.
On most days, one of our volunteers sits up there with a spinning wheel. She'll show you how wool was spun by hand, and then she'll let you have a go yourself.
By the way, you might hear people mention a model of the town as it was in 1850. That's not in the Archive Room any more, it's been moved down to the gift shop.
When we finish, you'll have free time. There's a guidebook on sale, but to be honest, most of what's in it I'll have told you already.
What I really would recommend is a walk along the canal path behind the mill. It's where the cotton barges used to unload, and it's lovely at this time of year.
And if you can, do come back on the first Sunday of a month, when the engine is running. It's a completely different experience when the whole building shakes.
Right, if everyone's ready, follow me down the stairs, and mind the second step.

title: Planning a presentation on cycling to campus
setting: Hai sinh viên ngành địa lý giao thông bàn kế hoạch cho bài thuyết trình về khảo sát việc đạp xe đến trường.
lines: Hi, Tom. Have you got half an hour to sort out the presentation? It's only two weeks away now.
Yeah, sure. I've brought the survey results with me.
Brilliant. I've been worried about it all week. I keep thinking we haven't got enough to say.
Honestly, I think we've got too much, if anything. We'll have to be quite strict about what goes in.
Great. So how many responses did we get in the end?
Well, 240 people started the questionnaire, but about thirty of them stopped halfway through. So really we've got 210 that we can use.
That's still more than the 180 we were aiming for. I'm pleased with that.
Me too. And the results themselves are quite interesting.
Did the online version work better than the paper one in the end?
Much better. Almost everyone did it on their phone. We only got about fifteen paper copies back.
Go on, what stood out for you?
I expected the number of students who cycle to be low, and it was, only about twelve percent. That didn't surprise me at all.
What I didn't expect was the reason people gave for not cycling. I assumed they'd say the hills, or the weather.
No. The number one reason was that there's nowhere safe to leave a bike. Hardly anyone mentioned the rain.
That really surprised me too, when I looked at the comments. The age of the cyclists was pretty much what I'd guessed, mostly postgraduates.
OK. What about the interviews? Should we play some of the recordings during the talk?
I'm not sure. We did most of them in the café, and the sound quality is terrible. You can hear the coffee machine over everything.
That's true. But some of the things people said were brilliant. It'd be a shame to lose them completely.
Agreed. Why don't we just pick a few short quotations and put them on a slide?
Perfect. That's much easier than editing audio, too.
Now, Dr Hassan gave us some feedback on the outline, didn't she?
She did. Her main point was that our draft spends far too long explaining how we carried out the survey. She wants that part cut down to a minute or so.
Fair enough. Didn't she also say something about comparing our results with another university?
She mentioned it, but she said it was optional. And honestly, we don't have time to find the data.
No. We were always going to finish with recommendations anyway, so that doesn't change.
Right. So shall we divide up the work? I'm happy to do the introduction. I've already written some notes for it.
Great, that's yours then. I'll do the charts, since I've got all the figures in my spreadsheet.
OK. And what about the map showing where the bike racks are? I could do that.
Actually, wait. You cycle in every day, so you know the campus much better than I do. It makes more sense for you to do it.
Fair point. I'll do the map as well, then.
Then there's the slide with the quotations.
We each did half of the interviews, so why don't we both choose the best quotes from our own ones and put them together?
Good idea. That's a joint job. And the recommendations?
I was thinking we should both write those too.

Hmm, I think it'll get messy with two people writing the same section. Since I'm doing the introduction, and the recommendations need to link back to it, why don't I draft them? You can comment afterwards.
That makes sense. So that's you.

title: The history of paper
setting: Bài giảng về lịch sử của giấy, từ Trung Quốc cổ đại đến ngành giấy hiện đại.
lines: Good morning. Today we're looking at a material most of us take completely for granted, and that's paper. I want to trace its journey from ancient China to the modern recycling plant.
Let's start with what people used before paper existed. In China, documents were written either on strips of bamboo, which were heavy and awkward to store, or on silk.
Silk was light and pleasant to write on, but it was extremely expensive, so it was only really used by the wealthy and by the imperial court.

The traditional story credits a court official called Cai Lun with inventing paper in the year 105. In fact, archaeologists have found fragments of paper that are older than that, so it's more accurate to say he improved and standardised the process.
According to the records, Cai Lun used tree bark, hemp, old rags, and even worn-out fishing nets. These were soaked and beaten into a pulp.
The wet pulp was then spread thinly onto a screen, a frame with fine cloth stretched across it, and left in the sun to dry. That basic method hasn't really changed in almost two thousand years.
For several centuries, the technique stayed largely within China and its neighbours. It reached the city of Samarkand, in Central Asia, in the eighth century.
The papermakers there faced a practical problem, which was that the plants used in China didn't grow locally. So instead of bark, they used linen rags, which were cheap and widely available.
There's a well-known story that the secret came west with Chinese papermakers who were captured in a battle in 751. Historians now doubt this, but the dates fit reasonably well.
From Samarkand, the craft spread to Baghdad, where a paper mill was operating by the end of the eighth century.
This had an enormous effect on how the state was run. Officials in Baghdad began to use paper for government records, partly because it was harder to alter than parchment without leaving a mark.
Paper arrived in Europe through Spain, where the first mills were set up in the twelfth century. But its reception was surprisingly cool.
Monks and lawyers didn't trust it. They preferred parchment, made from animal skin, because they believed it would last far longer. One emperor even banned paper for official documents.
Attitudes only really changed after the printing press appeared in the fifteenth century. Printers needed a cheap material in huge quantities, and parchment simply couldn't supply that.
To give you an idea of the scale, a single copy of a large Bible printed on parchment needed the skins of more than a hundred animals. On paper, the cost fell dramatically.

Now, this success created its own problem. By the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, demand was so high that there was a serious shortage of rags. Some mills even advertised, asking households to save their old clothes.
The solution came in the 1840s, when inventors in Germany and Canada found ways of making paper from wood pulp. Suddenly, paper became cheap enough for daily newspapers and school exercise books.
But wood pulp paper had a hidden weakness. Because of the chemicals used to process it, it contained acid, and over time this acid breaks the fibres down.
That's why so many books from the late nineteenth century have turned yellow and brittle, while some much older books printed on rag paper are still in excellent condition.
Libraries today spend a great deal of money treating these books to stop the damage. And since the 1980s, most good-quality paper has been made acid-free, so the problem is much smaller than it was.
Finally, what about paper today? Many people predicted that computers would create the paperless office. Office paper use has fallen, but overall the industry is still enormous.
The biggest use of paper now isn't printing at all. It's packaging, and the main driver of that is online shopping, with all those cardboard boxes arriving at our doors.
The good news is that paper is one of the most recycled materials we have. The fibres can be reused up to seven times before they become too short and weak to hold together.
After that, they're usually burned to produce energy. In our next session, we'll look at whether that's really as green as it sounds.

title: Coastal conservation volunteers
setting: Điều phối viên giới thiệu chương trình tình nguyện bảo vệ bờ biển cho nhóm tình nguyện viên mới.
lines: Morning, everyone, and thanks for coming along. I'm Liam, and I coordinate the Coastcare volunteer programme here at Banksia Bay. I'll run through how the programme works, and then there's time for questions.
The programme has been running for about twelve years now. We started with five people and a few rubbish bags, and these days we've got over two hundred volunteers on our list.
First, what are we actually trying to do? People often think we're mainly a beach-cleaning group, and yes, we do collect a lot of rubbish.
But our main goal is to protect the sand dunes. The dunes are what stop the sea from washing away the coast road, and they're also where most of our wildlife lives.
A quick note on age. Volunteers under eighteen are very welcome. You don't need to come with a parent, but we do need a consent form signed by one before your first session.
OK, let's go through the weekly timetable. You'll find it on the sheet in your folder, though some details are missing, so you might want to fill them in.
On Mondays we do the big beach clean. We provide the bags and the litter pickers, but please bring your own gloves. We used to hand them out, but people kept taking them home.
We weigh everything we collect, and the figures go to the local council. Last year it came to just under three tonnes, most of it plastic.
On Wednesdays it's planting. We grow native seedlings in our nursery, and then we plant them on the parts of the dunes that have been damaged by storms.
It's hard work, I won't pretend otherwise, but it's very satisfying to come back a few months later and see the plants holding the sand in place.
Friday is turtle nest monitoring, which is usually the most popular day. It starts early, at six. We'll meet at the lighthouse, not the car park, because that's much closer to the nesting area.
You'll walk along the beach with an experienced volunteer, checking the nests for any damage and recording what you see. Numbers on Fridays are limited, so put your name on the list in advance.
Then on Saturdays, we run a session where school groups visit and we show them around. Volunteers help to lead small groups of children, so it's great if you enjoy that kind of thing.
Now, what do you get out of it, apart from fresh air? Well, everyone receives a uniform T-shirt, so the public can see you're part of the team. You'll get that today, before you leave.
And once you've completed twenty hours, we'll give you a certificate, which a lot of students find useful for job applications.
I should say what we can't offer. We don't provide transport, I'm afraid, so you'll need to get here yourselves. And please bring your own lunch.
Some of you may have heard about a discount at the shops in town. That scheme ended last year, unfortunately.
A few rules, then. Photos are fine, and we love seeing them. But please never post the location of a turtle nest online. Sadly, people do go looking for them.
And even if your dog is very well behaved, please don't bring it on volunteer days. Dogs can smell the nests, and they frighten the birds.
You can walk on the dunes as long as you stay on the marked paths. And sunscreen is absolutely fine, in fact we insist on it.
Last thing. If you can't make a session, just send a text to the volunteer phone. You don't need to give a reason.
We'd just rather know, so the team leaders aren't waiting around on the beach for you at six in the morning.

title: A project on kelp farming
setting: Hai sinh viên sinh học biển thảo luận với giảng viên về đề tài nuôi tảo bẹ để hấp thụ carbon.
lines: Come in, both of you. So, you've chosen kelp farming as a way of capturing carbon. Tell me why you went for that topic.
Well, we'd both seen a documentary about kelp forests last year, and that got us interested.
But honestly, the main reason is that we both want to work in aquaculture after we graduate. So it felt like a project that would actually help us get a job.
And there's a lot of interest in it at the moment. Several companies are already selling carbon credits based on kelp farms.
There is, and that's exactly why it needs careful, critical work. Some of those claims are rather optimistic.
That's a very good reason. Now, I've read your draft. Let's start with the data. Where did your growth figures come from?
Mostly from three studies of kelp farms. They're all fairly recent, within the last five years.
Recent is good. The trouble is that all three were done off the coast of Norway. Kelp grows very differently in warmer water, so you can't really generalise from one region.
We did wonder about that. We thought the measurements might be the issue, but they all used the same method.
The method's fine. It's the location that worries me. And that leads me to your conclusion.
Is it too vague? We weren't sure how strong to make it.
Quite the opposite. You say kelp farming could solve the problem of carbon emissions. That's far more certain than your evidence allows. It does link to your data, but you've pushed it too far.
OK, so we need to tone it down.
Something like 'kelp farming may make a modest contribution' would be much closer to what the evidence shows.
That does sound more academic, actually.
Yes. And I think you need to be clearer about what happens to the carbon after the kelp is harvested. That's where a lot of these claims fall apart.
Right. Because if it's eaten, the carbon goes back into the atmosphere fairly quickly.
Exactly. And the same is true if it's used as fertiliser, which is where most farmed kelp in Europe actually ends up. Most of the carbon is released again within a year or two.
So the carbon is only really locked away if the kelp sinks to the deep ocean.
That's right, and nobody knows yet how much farmed kelp does that. Make that point clearly.
Would it help to include a diagram showing the carbon cycle? I think it'd be easier to follow than a long paragraph.
Yes, please do. And while we're talking about length, your literature review is too long. I'd cut it by around 500 words.
We could probably lose the section on the history of seaweed harvesting. It's interesting, but it doesn't really support our argument.
I agree. Keep the focus on carbon.
Now, quickly, the sources you've listed. What did you make of the government report?
It was easy to read, but it didn't really go into detail. It covers every kind of ocean farming in about twenty pages.
Yeah, it was too general to be much use for us, really.
And the website run by the seaweed industry association?
It had lots of figures, but obviously they want to sell kelp. Every single study they mention is positive. I didn't trust it.
And the journal article by Chen?
That was the best thing we found. The statistics were hard going at first, but once we got through them, it answered almost all our questions.
It was really useful. We should probably rely on it more.
Good. Then I suggest you do. And try to find at least one study from warmer waters, perhaps from Australia or South Africa, to deal with the problem we discussed earlier.
Excellent. Send me a new draft by the end of next week, and we'll meet again after that.

title: Urban heat islands
setting: Bài giảng về hiện tượng đảo nhiệt đô thị: nguyên nhân, đối tượng chịu ảnh hưởng và các giải pháp làm mát thành phố.
lines: Good afternoon. Today's topic is something many of you will have felt on a summer evening, even if you didn't have a name for it. It's called the urban heat island.
Put simply, cities are warmer than the countryside around them. On a calm summer day, the difference can be several degrees.
And it isn't only big capital cities. Even towns of fifty thousand people show the effect clearly, if you measure carefully.
The idea isn't new. In the early nineteenth century, an English chemist called Luke Howard kept careful temperature records in and around London.
He found that the city was warmer than the surrounding villages, which you might expect. But what was surprising was when the difference was greatest. It wasn't at midday, it was at night.
And that's still the pattern we see today. Cities heat up during the day, and then they're very slow to cool down after dark.
So why does this happen? You might think it's mainly the heat given off by cars, factories and air conditioners. That does contribute, but in most cities it's a fairly small part of the picture.
The main cause is the materials cities are built from. Concrete, brick and asphalt absorb the sun's energy during the day and store it, and then release it slowly through the night.
Compare that with a field or a forest. There, much of the sun's energy goes into evaporating water from the soil and from plants, rather than heating the ground.
Tall buildings make it worse by trapping that heat and blocking the wind, but the materials are the starting point.
Why does it matter? Higher temperatures mean more energy used for cooling, and worse air quality. But the most serious effect is on health.

Outdoor workers and young children are certainly at risk. However, studies of major heatwaves have consistently found that the highest death rates are among older people who live alone. They're often less aware of the danger and less likely to ask for help.
Climate change makes all of this more urgent. Heatwaves are becoming longer and more frequent, and more than half of the world's population now lives in cities.
So what can cities do? Let me go through some of the main approaches.
The first is the cool roof. This simply means painting a roof white or a very light colour, so that it reflects sunlight instead of absorbing it.
On a hot afternoon, a cool roof can be up to 30 degrees cooler than a dark one. It's cheap, and it's quick to do.
Several cities, including New York, have run programmes where volunteers paint thousands of roofs each summer.
There is a drawback, though. In places with cold winters, a reflective roof means the building gets less free warmth from the sun, so heating costs can go up.
The second approach is the green roof, which is covered in plants. Plants cool the air around them mainly through evaporation, as water passes out through their leaves.
Green roofs have another advantage. They hold rainwater and release it slowly, which helps to reduce flooding during heavy storms.
The downside is cost. A green roof is much more expensive than a cool roof, and many older buildings simply aren't strong enough to carry the weight of wet soil.
The third approach, and probably the most effective, is planting trees along streets. Trees provide shade for pedestrians and for buildings, and they cool the air too.
But choosing the right species is critical. Hotter summers usually mean less rain, so planners need trees that can survive drought.
A good example is the city of Medellín in Colombia. It created a network of green corridors along roads and streams, and in those areas, temperatures have fallen by about 2 degrees.
That may not sound like much, but on a dangerous day it can make a real difference.
The corridors also gave people pleasant routes for walking and cycling, which the city had not really expected.

To finish, one problem that all of these approaches share. Most cities only have temperature measurements from a few weather stations. What planners really need is better data at street level, so they know exactly where to act first.
That's where we'll pick up next week.

lines: Good morning, Harbour Lettings, Lucy speaking. How can I help?
Oh, hi. I saw your advert online and I'm looking for a flat to rent in the city. I've only just moved here, so I don't really know the areas yet.
No problem at all. I'll take a few details first, and then I can tell you what we've got. Could I have your name, please?
That's right. Most people get it right first time, which is nice.
And what do you do, Daniel? Landlords usually like to know.
Well, I trained as a teacher back in Brisbane, but I changed careers a few years ago. I'm a nurse now. I start at the children's hospital next month.
Lovely. So do you have an area in mind? A lot of hospital staff look around Eastfield, because it's so close.
Eastfield's a bit too busy for me, I think. A colleague told me the streets near the canal are quieter, and I could cycle along the towpath to work.
Yes, the canal area is very popular. How many bedrooms are you after?
I was going to say one, because it's just me. But my sister's planning to come over from Australia and stay for a few months, so I'd better make it two.
Two bedrooms, then. And what's your budget?
I was hoping to keep it under £900 a month, but from what I've seen online, that's not very realistic. Let's say £950 as an absolute maximum.
That's sensible for that area. Would that include bills?
No, I'm happy to pay the bills separately.
Fine. Is there anything the flat must have?
I'm not fussed about a garden or a parking space, because I haven't got a car. But I cycle everywhere, so I really need secure storage for my bike. I had one stolen last year.
Oh dear. I'll make a note of that. And is there anything you'd rather avoid?
I'd prefer not to be on the ground floor. I lived in a ground-floor flat once, and people walking past could see straight in. The top floor is fine, even without a lift.
OK. Well, actually, I think I've got something that might suit you. It's a two-bedroom flat on the second floor, and there's a locked bike shed at the back of the building.
That sounds promising. Where is it exactly?
It's 14 Ashby Road. That's A-S-H-B-Y. It's about five minutes' walk from the canal.
It's £925 a month, so just within your budget.
The current tenants leave at the end of October, and it'll be cleaned and ready from the first of November.
That works perfectly, actually. The contract on the room I'm renting now runs out around then.
Would you like to see it? I could do Friday afternoon.
I'm on a training course all day Friday. Is the weekend possible?
Saturday morning, then? Shall we say ten o'clock at the flat?
Great. And please bring some identification with you, so that we can start the application straight away if you like the place.
I'm afraid it has to be your passport, because you're new to the country. We need to check your right to rent.
No worries, I'll bring my passport. Thanks very much, Lucy.
You're welcome, Daniel. See you on Saturday.

title: Millbrook Summer Festival
setting: Điều phối viên lễ hội cộng đồng giới thiệu chương trình, sơ đồ khu vực và lời khuyên cho khách trên đài phát thanh địa phương.
lines: Good evening, and thanks for tuning in to Community Hour. I'm Megan Doyle, and I'm coordinating this year's Millbrook Summer Festival, which runs from Friday the twelfth to Sunday the fourteenth of July.
Tonight I want to give you a quick guide to what's on, where to find things, and how to make the most of the weekend.

First, the big change. For the past twenty years, the festival has been held in Victoria Park. Some of you have assumed we've moved because we've outgrown it, and it's true that the crowds get bigger every year.

But the real reason is that the council is putting in a new drainage system right across the park, and the ground will be dug up all summer. So this year we'll be on the grounds of Millbrook High School and in the streets around it.
Now, money. I'm pleased to say that entry to the festival site is still completely free, for adults as well as children, and that includes all the daytime music on the main stage.
The one exception is the two evening concerts on Friday and Saturday. Tickets for those are fifteen dollars, or ten for students, and you can buy them from the library.

We've also been overwhelmed by offers of help this year, which is wonderful. In fact, we have more than enough people for putting up the marquees on Thursday, and the St John's team are looking after first aid as usual.

Where we're really short is on keeping the site clean. If you can spare two hours to collect litter and empty the recycling bins, please sign up. You'll get a free festival T-shirt and a meal voucher.
So, what's new? Last year many of you asked for a dog show, and we did think about it, but the school doesn't allow animals on its playing fields.

The silent disco was so popular last year that it's back again. But the really new thing is that, for the first time, we're hosting a night market on Saturday, with food stalls run by local restaurants until eleven o'clock.
Let me tell you where things are, because the layout is quite different from the park.
The main stage is on the school field, facing the sports hall. Right next to the main stage you'll find the bar and the information tent.

The storytelling tent for younger children was going to be next to the main stage as well, but it's far too noisy there. So we've moved it to the library car park, which is much quieter and shaded by trees.
The farmers' market, with fruit, cheese and bread from local producers, will be down by the lake, where there's plenty of space for the vans to unload.
If the weather turns, don't worry about the dance competition. We've booked the sports hall for it, so it'll go ahead indoors whatever happens.
And the children's sports, the sack race, the egg and spoon race and so on, will be on the school field, at the far end, well away from the stage.
Finally, a few tips for getting there and staying comfortable.

There's no public parking at the school this year, and you can't book a space in advance, so please don't drive. Instead, take the free shuttle bus, which leaves from the railway station every fifteen minutes.
You'll be able to pay by card at every stall, so there's no need to carry lots of cash around.
We're also trying to cut down on plastic, so we won't be selling bottled water. Bring your own bottle and fill it up at one of the six water stations around the site.
As for the weather, the forecast is for a cool, cloudy weekend. So rather than sun hats, you might want to pack a light jacket for the evenings.
That's all from me. Full details, including a map, are on the festival website. See you there!

title: Coastal field trip report
setting: Hai sinh viên địa lý bàn về chuyến thực địa ở một làng ven biển và cách sửa từng phần của bài báo cáo.
lines: Hi Josh. Have you got a few minutes to talk about the field trip report? It's due in two weeks, and I'm starting to panic a bit.
Sure, Emma. Actually, I was going through my notes from Saltby this morning.
Great. Before we start, can I just say, I still can't get over that sea wall. I'd read that sea walls can make erosion worse further along the coast, but I didn't expect to see it so clearly.
You mean the stretch where the beach had completely disappeared?
Exactly. I knew the cliffs were retreating quickly, because the figures were in the background reading. But seeing how the wall had simply moved the problem down the coast was a real shock.
For me it was how empty the village felt. But I suppose that's because so many of the cottages are holiday homes now.
Which brings me to the interviews. I was a bit disappointed with them.
Me too. Not because people wouldn't talk. They were really friendly, and the recordings came out fine.
The trouble was that most of the people we stopped were visitors, not locals, so they didn't know much about how the coast had changed over the years.
Right. We only got three proper residents.
OK, so, the measurements. I've put all the cliff profiles into a spreadsheet.
Is there anything you're worried about?
Well, I wondered about the equipment at first, because the tape measure got soaked. But I checked our readings against last year's group, and they're consistent.
So the problem is more that we only had one week, in spring. Erosion is much worse during the winter storms, so our figures probably underestimate what happens over a whole year.
Yes, I think that's the real limitation. We had enough measuring points, twelve along a kilometre, which is what the tutor recommended.
Agreed. We should say that clearly in the discussion. Now, let's go through the sections. The introduction is quite long in my draft.
I read it. It's good, but it's nearly a thousand words, and half of it is general background on coastal processes that everyone on the course already knows.
Fair enough. I'll cut it down to about four hundred.
Then the methods. I think the text is fine as it is, but it would be much clearer if we put in some photos of us using the clinometer and the ranging poles.
Good idea. I took loads of pictures. I'll choose a few.
What about the results? There are so many tables.
I don't want to lose any data, but you're right, it's hard to read. Why don't we keep the summary graphs in the main text and put the full tables in an appendix?
Yes, that's what the handbook suggests anyway.
Now, the interviews. Given that we only spoke to three residents, I'm not sure it deserves a whole section of its own.
We could add it to the discussion, as extra evidence about the sea wall. The fisherman's comments would fit really well there.
So, we merge it with the discussion. OK.
I wasn't sure whether we're allowed to include recommendations for the council, like moving the cliff path. I don't want to get it wrong.
Let's check with Dr Hughes before we change anything. She'll know what the department expects.
Fine. I'll email her this afternoon. So, before we meet again on Thursday, what else needs doing?
I'll redraw the graphs, because the colours don't show up when you print them in black and white.
Good. And I'll find two or three academic sources on sea walls. Our reference list is a bit thin at the moment.
Should we contact the residents again, to get more detail?
Honestly, I don't think there's time. And we certainly can't go back to Saltby before the deadline.
True. What about the word count? Should we check that now?
Let's leave that until the final draft. There's no point yet.

title: Sleep and memory
setting: Bài giảng về khoa học giấc ngủ: các giai đoạn ngủ, vai trò của giấc ngủ với trí nhớ, tác hại của thiếu ngủ và đồng hồ sinh học của thanh thiếu niên.
lines: Good morning, everyone. Today we're continuing our series on the biology of everyday life, and the topic is sleep, and in particular, what sleep does for memory.

We spend roughly a third of our lives asleep. For a long time, scientists assumed that sleep was simply a period of rest, when the brain more or less switched off. We now know that's far from the truth.
Let me start with the structure of sleep. Over the night, we pass through several stages, from light sleep into deep sleep, and then into what's called REM sleep, REM standing for rapid eye movement.

Together, these stages make up a cycle. You'll sometimes read that a cycle takes an hour, but in adults a full cycle lasts about ninety minutes, and we normally go through four or five of them each night.

In deep sleep, the brain produces large, slow electrical waves. It's also the time when the body carries out a lot of physical repair. For example, most of our growth hormone is released during deep sleep, which is one reason children need so much of it.
REM sleep is quite different. The brain becomes almost as active as when we're awake, and this is when most vivid dreaming happens.
Researchers increasingly believe that REM sleep plays a central role in processing emotions, helping us to come to terms with difficult experiences from the day.
So how do we know that sleep helps memory? Some of the most convincing evidence comes from animal studies.
In one well-known series of experiments, researchers recorded the activity of individual neurons in rats while the animals learned to find their way through a maze.

Each location in the maze triggered a particular pattern of firing. Then, when the rats slept afterwards, the same patterns appeared again, in the same order, as if the brain were replaying the route, only much faster than the original journey.
Similar effects have been found in humans. In a typical study, volunteers learn a list of word pairs at midday. Half of them then stay awake, while the other half have a nap of about an hour.
When they're tested later in the afternoon, the group who had the nap remember significantly more of the pairs, even though both groups spent the same amount of time away from the material.
And sleep doesn't just help with facts. During light sleep, the brain produces short bursts of activity known as sleep spindles.
People who produce more spindles after practising a task tend to improve more at motor skills, things like typing a sequence on a keyboard, or playing a melody on the piano.
Now, what happens when we don't get enough sleep? Here the findings are rather alarming.

In one experiment, students were kept awake for a whole night and then asked to learn a set of pictures. Compared with students who had slept normally, their ability to form new memories fell by around forty per cent.
Brain scans help to explain why. The hippocampus, a small, curved structure deep in the brain that acts as a kind of inbox for new memories, became much less active in the sleep-deprived group.
Interestingly, the area involved in emotional reactions became more active, which may explain why tired people are often more irritable.
Finally, I'd like to apply some of this to a group many of you were part of not so long ago: teenagers.
It's easy to assume that teenagers stay up late simply because of their phones, and screens certainly don't help. But there's a biological reason too.
During adolescence, the body clock shifts. The brain starts to release melatonin, the hormone that makes us feel sleepy, around two hours later than it does in children or adults.

So a fifteen-year-old who's told to go to bed at nine may genuinely be unable to fall asleep. Yet most schools still start early in the morning, which means many teenagers are constantly short of sleep.
Several school districts in the United States have experimented with later start times, sometimes by as little as an hour.
The results have been encouraging. Students got more sleep, and grades went up slightly. But perhaps the clearest improvement was in attendance, with far fewer students missing classes.
Next week, we'll look at the other side of the coin: what happens to the body clock when we fly across time zones or work night shifts. Thank you.

title: Booking a cycling tour
setting: Một du khách gọi điện cho công ty tour xe đạp để đặt chuyến đạp xe có hướng dẫn viên cho nhóm.
lines: Good afternoon, Green Valley Cycle Tours, Tom speaking.
Hi there. I'm calling about booking one of your guided bike tours. I'm visiting the area with some friends next month.
Lovely. Do you know which tour you're interested in?
We looked at the Castle Trail on your website, because it goes past the old castle. But the reviews say there are some pretty steep climbs.
There are. It's about forty kilometres, with a lot of hills. If you'd like something more relaxed, the Lakeside Trail is flat almost the whole way, and it's only twenty-five kilometres.
That sounds much more like us. Let's go with the Lakeside Trail.
Great. And how many people will there be?
There were going to be four of us, but one friend has had to drop out because of work. So, three.
Three adults. And what date were you thinking of?
We arrive on Friday the 14th of June, so could we do it on Saturday the 15th?
Let me just check. Yes, Saturday the 15th is fine. We've still got places.
Perfect. Now, about the bikes. Two of us are fine on a normal bike, but my mother is coming too, and she hasn't cycled for years.
In that case, I'd suggest an electric bike for her. It gives you a bit of help with the pedalling, so she won't get tired. There's no extra charge.
Oh, that's great. She'll love that.
Can I take your name, please?
Yes, it's Rachel Okafor. That's O-K-A-F-O-R.
Thank you. And where would you like to meet? We usually start from our shop, but we can meet groups in town.
Then the easiest place is outside the museum. It's just across the square from the cathedral, and there's room for our van to stop.
We provide a picnic lunch at the halfway point. Does anyone have any special dietary requirements?
Yes, my friend can't eat wheat, so she'll need a gluten-free lunch. The rest of us will eat anything.
No problem. I'll make a note of that.
And can I just check what the price covers? It says sixty-five pounds per person on the website.
That includes the bike hire, a helmet, the guide and the lunch. The tour also stops at Holm Gardens, and your entry there is included too.
The only extra is the boat trip on the lake at the end, which is optional. That's eight pounds each, and you pay for it on the day.
OK. Is there anything we should bring?
You don't need any special clothing. Some people ask about padded shorts, but our saddles are very comfortable.
The weather by the lake can change very quickly, though, so I'd definitely bring a waterproof jacket. There's a café at the gardens, and they take cards, so you won't need cash.
Good to know. And how do I pay?
We take a deposit of twenty pounds per person. Normally I'd take your card details over the phone, but our card machine isn't working today.
So I'll email you a link instead, and you can pay online. What's your email address?
It's rachel dot okafor at mailbox dot com.
Thanks. You'll get it within the hour, and once it's paid, your booking is confirmed.
Wonderful. Thanks so much for your help, Tom.

title: University Careers Fair briefing
setting: Cán bộ trung tâm hướng nghiệp của trường đại học giới thiệu hội chợ việc làm sắp tới cho sinh viên.
lines: Hi everyone, and welcome to this short briefing. I'm Liam Carter from the Careers Service, and I'm going to run through what you need to know about next week's Careers Fair.

Some of you came to the fair last year, so you'll notice a couple of changes. Last year we tried running part of the event online, but to be honest, very few students or employers used it, so we've gone back to a fully in-person fair.
What is new is that the fair now runs over two days, Wednesday and Thursday, rather than just one. That means more employers, over a hundred and twenty this time, and a lot less crowding.
The fair is open to students in every year, as it always has been, so please don't think it's only for final-year students. Plenty of first-years find summer internships here.
Now, before you come, please register through the Careers app. You'll get a QR code on your phone, which you show at the door.
You can also register at the entrance desk on the day, but last year the queue there was over half an hour long, so it's much better to do it in advance. And there's no need to email us.
Let me explain where everything is, because the fair is spread across several buildings this year.
The Main Hall is where you'll find most of the employers from banking, retail and the public sector. That's always the busiest area.
Engineering and technology companies need more space for their displays, and some of them bring robots and even a small racing car, so they'll be in the Sports Centre.
If you'd like someone to look at your CV, our advisers will be in the Library Foyer on both days. Just turn up. It only takes about ten minutes.

We'd originally planned to hold the mock interviews in the foyer too, but it was far too noisy, so they've moved to the Blue Room, on the first floor of the Arts Building. Those you do need to book, through the app.
And if you're thinking about a master's or a PhD rather than going straight into work, the postgraduate study team will be in the Student Union, next to the café.
Now, a bit of advice about talking to employers. The best conversations happen when students have done their homework.
So before the fair, look through the list of exhibitors, pick five or six, and find out what they actually do. Employers can tell straight away if you've researched their company.
Second, think about how you'll introduce yourself. Prepare a few sentences: your name, your course, and the kind of role you're interested in. It sounds simple, but it really helps if you're nervous.
You don't need to bring a pile of printed CVs. Most employers now prefer you to scan their QR code and upload your CV directly.
And although it's tempting, I'd avoid asking about salary in a first conversation. You'll have plenty of chances to discuss that later in the process.
Oh, and please don't spend all your time collecting free pens and bags from the stands. It's much better to have three good conversations than twenty quick ones.
Finally, there's a programme of talks running alongside the fair. Most of them are in the main lecture theatre, and you don't need to book.

We know not everyone can attend, so two of the talks will be recorded and put on the Careers website afterwards. Those are Starting your own business, on Wednesday, and Making the most of LinkedIn, on Thursday.
We wanted to record Working abroad as well, but the speaker preferred not to be filmed, so if that one interests you, make sure you're there in person.
Graduate schemes explained and Careers in the public sector will be live only, but the slides will be available on request.
Right, that's everything from me. Are there any questions?
