title: Student travel survey
setting: Hai sinh viên hoàn thiện bảng khảo sát về cách sinh viên đi lại đến trường cho môn quy hoạch giao thông.
lines: So, Sam, we really need to get the travel survey finalised this week if we want enough time to analyse the results.
I know. Shall we start with the numbers? In the proposal we said we'd aim for a hundred and fifty responses.
We did, but Dr Morgan said that's too small if we want to compare different groups of students. She suggested two hundred as a minimum.
Two hundred, then. That's quite a lot. We'll need some kind of incentive.
I was thinking about offering free coffee, but the café wouldn't agree to it. The campus bookshop, though, said they'd give us a book voucher worth thirty pounds.
Brilliant. So everyone who completes the survey can enter a prize draw for the voucher.
Exactly. And we need to keep it short. People give up if it takes too long.
My cousin did a survey last year that took fifteen minutes, and hardly anyone finished it. Ours should take no more than five minutes.
Agreed. Five minutes maximum. Now, are we still doing paper questionnaires as well as the online version?
I've changed my mind about that. The printing isn't the problem, because the department will pay for it.
It's that someone has to type every answer into the computer afterwards, and with two hundred forms, that would take days.
True. Online only, then. The software puts everything straight into a spreadsheet.
Did you see Dr Morgan's comments on the draft questions?
Yes. She was mostly happy, but she said question seven wouldn't work.
The one about cost and journey time?
That's the one. We asked, is your journey cheap and quick? But if someone's journey is cheap but slow, they don't know how to answer.
Of course. So we split it into two separate questions.
I was worried she'd say the question about income was too personal, but she thought it was fine, as long as it's optional.
Good. And what did you think of the pilot? I haven't had time to look at the results properly.
Well, twelve people did it, which is exactly what we planned. The surprising thing was that nobody drives. They all walk, cycle or take the bus.
But that's probably just because they're all our friends from halls.
Quite a few people missed out the questions on the second page. I think they didn't realise they had to scroll down.
We can fix that by putting each question on its own screen.
Good idea. Now, how are we going to reach people? We need a proper mix of students, not just our friends.
For first-years, I think posters in the halls of residence would work best. Nearly all of them live there.
Couldn't we just use social media?
We could, but there are so many posts on the student groups that ours would just disappear.
Fair enough. What about postgraduates? They hardly ever come to the main campus.
Each department has an email list for its research students. I'll ask the department secretaries to send the link out for us.
Great. And for international students, the International Society has nearly a thousand members, and the president is in my seminar group.
I'm sure she'd share it at their events and in their newsletter.
Perfect. Then that just leaves part-time students. They're the hardest group, because most of them only come in during the evenings.
I suppose we could ask lecturers to mention it in class, but they're so busy.
I think we'd have more luck if we went along ourselves. We could stand by the reception desk at the evening centre with a tablet and ask people as they arrive.
Two evenings should be enough. Let's do that next week.
Great. I'll update the questions tonight and send you the new version, so you can check it before we send it to Dr Morgan.
Sounds good. If she's happy with it, we could launch the survey on Monday and close it at the end of the month.

title: Renewable building materials
setting: Bài giảng về vật liệu xây dựng tái tạo: tre, gỗ ghép chéo (CLT) và vật liệu từ sợi nấm.
lines: Good afternoon. In the last session, we looked at the environmental cost of conventional building materials. Today I want to turn to the alternatives, and specifically to what are often called renewable materials.

Let's begin with a definition, because the word renewable is used rather loosely. Some people use it to mean any material that can be recycled many times, like steel or glass. That's not what I mean today.

A renewable material, in the sense I'll be using, is one that comes from a living source and can be regrown within a human lifetime, ideally much faster than that. So that means timber, bamboo, straw, and some newer materials made from fungi.
Why does this matter? Concrete and steel are extremely energy-intensive to produce. Cement manufacture alone accounts for roughly eight per cent of global carbon dioxide emissions.
Plants, by contrast, absorb carbon as they grow, and much of that carbon stays locked inside the material for the whole life of the building.
Let's start with bamboo. It's technically a grass, not a tree, and its great strength, if you'll forgive the pun, is its speed of growth.
Some species can grow almost a metre in a single day, and a bamboo plantation can be harvested after three to five years, compared with several decades for most timber.
It's also remarkably strong in tension, which is why it's been used for scaffolding in parts of Asia for centuries.

Of course, bamboo has its limitations. It grows mainly in tropical regions, so shipping it to Europe or North America adds both cost and emissions. And it needs chemical treatment to protect it from insects and rot.
The second material, and the one that's really transforming the industry, is cross-laminated timber, usually called CLT.

CLT panels are made by gluing layers of wood together, with each layer placed at right angles to the one below. This makes the panels very stable and strong in both directions, so they can be used for walls and floors.

For many years, architects who wanted to build tall timber buildings met strong resistance. It wasn't really about cost, which was competitive, and there's plenty of sustainably managed forest. The real worry was fire.

It seems obvious that wood burns. But tests have shown that thick CLT panels char on the outside, and that charred layer actually protects the wood inside, so the structure keeps its strength for a predictable length of time.
As a result, building regulations in many countries have now been revised.
The results can be impressive. In Norway, there's an eighteen-storey timber tower that contains apartments, offices and a hotel, with a restaurant on the top floors.
Another advantage is on the building site itself. Because the panels are cut to size in a factory, construction is faster and quieter, and there's far less waste than with concrete.
Now to the most experimental material on my list: mycelium. Mycelium is the network of fine threads that forms the root-like part of fungi.
What we normally call a mushroom is really just the fruit. The mycelium is the main body of the organism, spreading underground.
To make building products, manufacturers mix mycelium with agricultural waste, typically straw or the husks left over from cereal crops.
They put the mixture into a mould, and over about a week the fungus grows through it and binds it into a solid block. The block is then heated, which kills the fungus and stops it growing.
The result is very light, and it can be composted at the end of its life.

At the moment, it isn't strong enough to hold up a building. Its main use is in insulation panels, where its lightness and its ability to trap air are real advantages. Some companies also make packaging from it, as a replacement for polystyrene.

The big problem researchers are trying to solve is that mycelium materials absorb moisture. In a damp climate, that can cause the material to break down, so for now it needs a protective coating or has to be used indoors.
So, to sum up, none of these materials will replace concrete and steel entirely in the near future. But together, they could dramatically reduce the carbon footprint of new buildings.
For next week, please read the case study on the Norwegian tower, and come prepared to discuss its costs.

title: Hiring field recording equipment
setting: Một nhà sản xuất phim tài liệu người Úc gọi điện cho công ty cho thuê thiết bị thu âm chuyên dụng để đặt máy, đặt cọc và hẹn giao hàng.
lines: Good afternoon, Fieldsound Hire, Tom speaking.
Oh, hi, Tom. I'm calling about hiring some recording gear for a shoot next month. I sent an enquiry through your website, but I'm honestly not sure it went through.
Let me have a look. What name would it be under?
Right, I've got a Pendergast here, P-E-N-D-E-R-G-A-S-T, from last Tuesday. Would that be you?
That'll be me, but you've lost the R. It's P-R-E-N, then D-E-R, then G-A-S-T. People drop it all the time, so don't worry.
Sorry about that, I'll correct it now. So, what can we do for you?
We're making a short documentary about seabirds on the Cornish coast, and I'd pencilled in a parabolic dish, you know, the big reflector, for picking up calls from a distance.
We do have those, yes. Can I ask where you'll be setting up, though?
Well, that's the thing. I've since been told the best spot is a forty-minute scramble up a cliff path, and lugging a dish that size up there sounds like a nightmare.

It would be, frankly, and they catch the wind like a sail. For that kind of location most people go for a shotgun microphone instead. It's far more directional than you'd expect, and it fits in a backpack.
OK, let's go with the shotgun, then. Forget the dish. And I'll need a recorder to go with it.
Sure. Our most popular field recorder is the R45, but if you're after birdsong, I'd steer you towards the R54. It has lower self-noise, which matters when the sound you want is faint.
Sorry, which way round? Forty-five or fifty-four?
Fifty-four is the one I'd recommend. The R54. It's a bit pricier, but not dramatically.
Fine, the R54 it is. Now, dates. I'd originally said the thirteenth of March for delivery, I think?
That's what I've got, yes. Delivery on the thirteenth.
Could we bring it forward? Our presenter's only free earlier in the week, so the crew's now arriving on the eleventh, and we'd want everything there when they turn up.
The eleventh shouldn't be a problem. And you'd want it until when?
The nineteenth. That's a Friday. Is there a particular time it has to be back by?
It used to be five o'clock, but since the courier changed their collection round, it's midday on Fridays. So, before noon on the nineteenth.
Noon. Got it. I'll make sure someone's packed everything up the night before.
Great. Now, because this is specialist kit, we do take a refundable deposit. For the shotgun and the R54 together, that would normally be £600.
Ouch. Is there any flexibility on that? We hired some lights from you last year, if that helps.
It does, actually. Returning customers with no damage claims get twenty-five per cent off the deposit, so that brings it down to £450.
That's much better. Can I just put that on a credit card?
I'm afraid not, not for deposits over £400. The card companies make refunds awkward. It'll need to be a bank transfer, and we release it within five working days of the kit coming back.
A bank transfer's fine. Our accounts team can sort that out. What about insurance? Do I have to take yours?
Unless your production has its own equipment cover, yes. It's £12 a day. Sorry, no, I'm reading from the old price list. It went down to £9.50 in January.
Nine fifty a day. I'll check our own policy, but I suspect we'll take yours, just for peace of mind. Cliffs and salt water, you know.
Very wise. Now, the delivery address.
It's a holiday cottage near Sennen, so the postcode's probably the most useful thing. It's T-R-1-9, then 6-B-X. No, hang on, I've got the booking email here. It's P, not B. P for Peter.
That's it. The cottage is called Gull's Rest, but apparently the sat nav gets confused, so the driver should go by the postcode rather than the name.
Noted. Is there anything else the driver needs to know?

Yes, the mobile signal's pretty patchy round there. Could they give us a ring when they're about half an hour away? Actually, no. The lane's single-track, and they'll be stuck behind tractors anyway. Make it twenty minutes.
Twenty minutes before arrival. I'll put that in the notes. And who should they ask for?
Me, or our sound recordist, Declan. One of us will definitely be there.
Lovely. I'll email a confirmation within the hour, with our bank details for the deposit.
Brilliant. Thanks so much, Tom, you've been really helpful.

title: Orientation at Harrowby Mill
setting: Một hướng dẫn viên giới thiệu lịch sử, quá trình trùng tu và vị trí các tiện ích trong khu di sản nhà máy cũ Harrowby Mill cho đoàn khách tham quan.
lines: Morning, everyone, and welcome to Harrowby Mill. I'm Dana, I'm one of the volunteer guides, and before you head off on your own, I'll give you a bit of background and, more usefully, tell you where everything is, because the site's grown a lot.

So, first, the obvious question people ask: what did this place actually make? Most visitors assume it was a corn mill, I mean, there's a water wheel, so you'd think flour, right? But when it opened in 1791, it was spinning flax for linen thread.

It only switched to paper in the 1880s, once the linen trade had collapsed, and that's the period most of the machinery you'll see dates from. So, flax first, paper later, and, as far as we can tell, never grain at all.
Now, some of you will have read that the restoration's running about two years behind schedule. People tend to assume that's money, but actually the lottery grant came through in full, and on time.
And yes, we did find a colony of bats in the roof, which made the local paper, but that held things up by a few weeks, nothing more. The real sticking point is people.
There are hardly any millwrights left who know how to rebuild a wooden gear train, and we've had to wait our turn for the two we found.
OK, so, finding your way around. You're standing in the main courtyard right now, with the clock tower behind me.
The ticket office is just under the tower, and that's also where our first-aid point is, so if anyone so much as twists an ankle, head there.
The café. If you've been here before, you'll remember it in the old counting house, that's the low brick building on your left.
It moved last spring, and it's now up in the former drying loft, at the top of the main mill, where the paper used to be hung. Take the lift, it's quite a climb otherwise.

Bike hire. Our leaflet still says it's next to the visitor car park, and it was, until the council resurfaced it. It's now been moved down beside the weir, which is actually handier, because the towpath starts right there.
The children's workshop, this week it's paper marbling, is in the walled yard behind the forge.
Normally, if it rained, we'd shift it into the basement of the counting house, but that's being re-floored, so the plan is to stay put under the awnings whatever the weather does.

And speaking of that basement, it's not entirely closed. The far end, the bit that's already finished, is where we've hung the new exhibition of photographs of the mill workers, mostly women and children, from about 1900. It's quite moving, honestly. Do take a look.

Picnics. You're very welcome to bring your own food. A lot of people try to set up beside the old water wheel because it's so photogenic, but you'll get soaked, the spray carries a surprisingly long way.
The picnic area is across the canal, at the far end of the footbridge, and there are benches and bins there.
Right, just a couple of requests before I let you go. Dogs are fine anywhere outside, and in the café, as long as they're on a lead. And you can bring food in, as I said.

In the loom gallery, please don't use flash. Some of those dyed linen samples are over two hundred years old, and the colours fade incredibly quickly under bright light. Ordinary photos without the flash are absolutely fine.
And outside, I know it's tempting, but please don't climb onto the sluice gates, or even lean over them to get a picture of the wheel. They're original, and they're not built to take anyone's weight.

Oh, and the ducks. For years we asked people not to feed them at all, but the wildlife trust's told us that's unnecessary. Just bring seed rather than bread, and there's a dispenser by the shop if you've forgotten.

And one last thing, the loom demonstration. It's at half eleven, not eleven as it says on your ticket, because our weaver's train is running late. That's about it. Enjoy your visit, and come and find me if you've got questions.

title: Designing a study on phone notifications
setting: Ba sinh viên ngành tâm lý học và giảng viên hướng dẫn tranh luận về cách thiết kế nghiên cứu xem thông báo điện thoại ảnh hưởng thế nào đến việc ôn thi.
lines: Right, so you've sent me a one-page outline on notifications and revision. Before we get into the detail, tell me where you've got to, because I sense from the email that you're not all on the same page.

That's fair. The question's settled, I think: whether incoming notifications, even ones you don't open, reduce how much students retain when they're revising. Where we've stalled is how to actually test it.

I'd still argue for a lab study. You bring people in, give them a passage to learn, have phones buzz at fixed intervals for half the group, and then test recall. It's clean. You know exactly what caused what.

Clean, sure, but it's a bit artificial, isn't it? Nobody revises for twenty minutes in a cubicle with a researcher next door. The moment people know they're being watched, they behave like model students.
OK, but every lab study has that problem, and we'd be comparing two groups who are both being watched, so it cancels out.

Does it, though? I mean, I'm not sure it does. If the people whose phones buzz are being observed, they might make a bigger effort to ignore them than they would at home. So the effect could shrink in the lab, not just shift.
That's a sharp point, Isla. It's not simply noise that affects both groups equally. It interacts with the very thing you're manipulating. Kofi, does that change your mind?
Partly. I'd still rather have a small effect I can trust than a big one I can't explain. But yes, I take the point that the lab might understate it.
Which is why I keep coming back to a diary study. Students log their revision sessions for two weeks, and an app records every notification automatically, so we're not relying on memory.
And how would you measure retention?

Well, originally I thought we'd just ask them to rate how much they'd taken in. But, sorry, I've gone off that. Self-ratings are hopeless, people who feel distracted mark themselves down regardless. So, a short quiz at the end of each session, on whatever they'd been revising.
But then the quizzes aren't comparable. One person's revising organic chemistry, someone else is doing French verbs. You can't line those scores up.
You can if you compare each person with themselves, sessions with lots of notifications against sessions with few.
Within-subject comparison. That does handle Isla's objection rather neatly, actually. What it doesn't handle is direction of cause. Sorry, go on, Kofi, you were about to say that.

Yeah, exactly that. Maybe on days people are already struggling with the material, they're more likely to leave their phone on, or check it. So the notifications might be a symptom rather than the cause.
Which is why I suggested combining them. A short lab phase to establish whether there's an effect at all, and then the diary to see whether it holds up in real life.

In principle I like that, but be realistic. You've got one term. Two data collection phases, two ethics applications, two lots of analysis. I've seen groups try that and end up with two half-finished studies.
Hmm. So you'd say pick one?
I'd say pick one design and do it properly, and use the limitations section to say what the other would add. Examiners respect a modest study that knows its own weaknesses.
Then I suppose the diary study's out. The app alone would take weeks to set up, and I don't think the department would even let us collect notification data from people's phones.
So we're back to the lab. Good.
Fine, but can we at least make it less sterile? Use the library's group study rooms rather than the testing cubicles, and let people bring their own revision material instead of our passage.
No, if everyone brings their own material, we're back to scores we can't compare. I'm happy with the study rooms, but the passage has to be the same for everyone.
I'd agree with Kofi there. Keep the material fixed. What you can do is choose a passage that resembles real coursework rather than something dry and invented.
What about the phones themselves? I'd assumed we'd use a lab phone, but if it's not their own phone, the notifications don't mean anything to them. Nobody cares about a stranger's message.
I'll grant you that one. Their own phones, then, but we'd need a way to trigger notifications.
A messaging group they join for the session. We post at set times. It's simple and nobody has to install anything.
That's workable. Just make sure the consent form says exactly what will be sent, and when. Right, I think you've got a design. Isla, can you rewrite the outline by Friday?

items.why: Isla: "can we at least make it less sterile? Use the library's group study rooms". Kofi chỉ đồng ý phần phòng học, không phải người đề xuất.

items.why: Kofi: "the passage has to be the same for everyone". Tutor đồng ý nhưng không có trong lựa chọn; Isla lại muốn cho mang tài liệu riêng.

title: The acoustics of historic concert halls
setting: Bài giảng đại học về âm học của các phòng hòa nhạc lịch sử: thời gian vang, hình dáng hộp giày, vật liệu, khán giả và ảnh hưởng ngược lại lên cách sáng tác.
lines: Today I want to look at why a handful of concert halls built in the late nineteenth century are still, more or less by consensus, regarded as the finest acoustic spaces in the world, and why, for a long time, nobody could quite explain it.
The obvious starting point is reverberation time, that's the time it takes for a sound to decay by sixty decibels once the source stops.
For orchestral music, the figure most acousticians aim for in a full hall is around two seconds. Much less and the sound feels dry; much more and the detail blurs.
Now, the curious thing is that the great halls were designed with almost no theory at all.
Wallace Sabine's formula relating reverberation to volume and absorption only appeared around 1900, so the architects of the earlier halls were working largely by imitation.
They copied rooms that sounded good, and, frankly, they got lucky.
What they copied, above all, was a shape: the so-called shoebox, a long, narrow, high rectangle. And the reason it works isn't really the length, it's the narrowness.
Sound from the stage strikes the side walls early and arrives at the listener's ears from the side.
And those lateral reflections, as we call them, are what produce a sense of envelopment, the feeling of being surrounded by the music rather than looking at it through a window.
Our brains read tiny differences between what the two ears receive as a sign that the sound is coming from all around us.
Compare that with the fan-shaped halls that became fashionable in the mid-twentieth century.

They were wonderful for sightlines, and they let you seat far more people, but the side walls splay away from the stage, so the early reflections tend to come from the front instead, and the sound, well, it feels distant, however loud it is.

The second ingredient is surface. Those halls are covered in what an architect at the time would have called ornament: plaster mouldings, coffered ceilings, statues in niches, rows of balcony fronts. We used to think of this as decoration. Acoustically, it's anything but.

All that relief breaks up reflected sound and scatters it in many directions, which is what we call diffusion. Without it, a flat wall acts like a mirror and you get harsh, distinct echoes. With it, the reflected energy arrives as a smooth, continuous wash.
Materials matter too, though not in the way people sometimes assume. There's a popular idea that wood makes a hall resonate like a violin. It doesn't, really. What matters is mass.
The best halls have thick plaster laid directly onto masonry, which reflects low frequencies instead of absorbing them, so the bass stays warm.

Thin wooden panelling with an air gap behind it, by contrast, actually soaks up the bass. So the much-admired wood in some modern halls is, acoustically speaking, often just a veneer glued onto concrete.

The third element, and it's one designers consistently underestimated, is the audience. A seated person absorbs a great deal of sound, so a hall that sounds glorious at a rehearsal can sound noticeably dead on the night.
That's why modern seats are upholstered to absorb roughly what a person would, so that the acoustic barely changes whether a seat's taken or not.

And it's also, incidentally, why the size of the older halls is so modest. Most hold fewer than two thousand people. Push much beyond that and you have to make the room wider, and once you widen it, you lose those lateral reflections I mentioned.

Which brings me to a point that's sometimes overlooked: the influence ran both ways. Composers wrote for the rooms they knew. In the very resonant churches of earlier centuries, harmonies had to change slowly, or successive chords would smear into one another.
Whereas the drier eighteenth-century court rooms suited quick, intricate passages.
Some historians go further and argue that the lush, sustained orchestral writing of the late Romantic period was, in effect, composed for the shoebox.
I'd put it a bit more cautiously, but the correspondence is hard to dismiss.

Finally, measurement. For decades, acousticians tested halls by firing a starting pistol on stage and recording the decay. Nowadays we use a sine sweep, a tone that rises steadily through the whole frequency range, which gives a far cleaner result even with background noise.
But I'd stress that the numbers have never been the whole story.
In the end, the reputation of a hall rests on the judgement of the musicians who play in it, and they will tell you that what they value most is being able to hear one another on stage.
We'll pick that up next week.

title: Joining a community orchestra
setting: Một người chơi đàn gọi điện cho thư ký dàn nhạc cộng đồng để hỏi về việc gia nhập, phí thành viên và buổi thử giọng.
lines: Hello, Westbridge Community Orchestra, Clare speaking.
Oh, hi, Clare. Um, I got this number off a poster in the library. I'm, well, I'm interested in joining, if you're taking new people at the moment?
We are, yes, though it depends a bit on the section, to be honest. What do you play?
So I started on violin as a kid, and I do still play it, but I've been doing a lot more viola for the last few years. I sort of drifted over.
Right. Well, I'll be frank with you, the violins are rather oversubscribed at the moment. There's a waiting list as long as your arm.
Violas we're crying out for. We lost two at the end of last season, one moved away and the other, well, retired, I suppose you'd call it.
Then let's go with viola. That's where I'd rather be anyway, if I'm honest.
Lovely. Let me just open up a form. Can I take your name?
Sure, it's Rhys, R-H-Y-S, and the surname's Aylward.
No, everyone does that. It's A-Y-L, then W-A-R-D.
A-Y-L-W-A-R-D. Got it, thanks. Now, have you had a chance to look at the membership options on our website?
I had a quick glance, but I'm not sure I took it all in. There were three, weren't there?

That's right. Full membership means you play in all four concerts and come to every rehearsal. Associate is for people who can only commit to a couple of concerts a year. And then supporter, which is non-playing.
Hmm. I travel for work quite a bit, so every single rehearsal might be pushing it. I mean, I'd love to say full, but I'd probably just end up letting people down.
Plenty of our players are in the same boat, so don't worry.
Yeah, I'll be realistic and go for associate. I can always upgrade later, can't I?
You can, at any point in the season. So the associate fee is £95 for the year.
Oh, I thought the website said £110.
That was last year's figure, I'm afraid the site's a bit behind. The committee brought it down in September. Full is £140, just for comparison.
Well, that's a pleasant surprise. And, sorry, the poster mentioned an audition. How formal is that? I haven't done one since uni.

Oh, it's very relaxed. You play a short piece of your own choice, five minutes or so, and then there's a bit of sight-reading. We used to ask for scales as well, but we dropped those a couple of years ago.
Thank goodness. Scales were always my weak spot. Sight-reading I can cope with.
Now, the string auditions are on Wednesday the twelfth, and I've got a slot at 7:15.
7:15... the thing is, I'm not back from Leeds until about seven that day. It'd be really tight.
Hang on, let me have a look. Ah, actually, the conductor's asked to run a bit later anyway, so there's a slot at 8:15. Would that suit you better?
Much better, yes. Put me down for that one.
Done. And it won't be in the main hall, because that's being rewired. It'll be in the Garden Room, round the back of St Anne's. Follow the signs from the car park.
OK. And do I need to bring anything apart from the viola?
Do bring your own music stand, if you've got one. We've got plenty of chairs, obviously, but stands have a habit of walking off.
Ha, fair enough. What about copies of my piece for the panel?
No, they won't need those. Now, assuming all goes well, rehearsals are on Thursday evenings, from seven till half past nine.
Thursdays? I'm sure the poster said Tuesdays.
It did, and that's a poster we really need to take down. We moved to Thursdays in the summer when the hall changed its bookings.
Right. And parking, is there anywhere nearby? I'll have the viola and a stand, so I don't really fancy a long walk.
There's the supermarket on the corner, but they charge after six, so most of us use the leisure centre on Kemp Street. It's free in the evenings and it's only a couple of minutes away.
Brilliant. Last thing, is there any chance of getting hold of the music early? I'm a slow learner.
Not from me, I'm afraid. Our librarian looks after all the parts, so I'll pass your details on and she'll email you the viola parts once you're in.
That's great. Thanks so much, Clare, you've been really helpful.
My pleasure, Rhys. See you on the twelfth.

title: Changes to the city cycle scheme
setting: Trên chương trình radio địa phương, một cán bộ giao thông giải thích những thay đổi của hệ thống xe đạp công cộng trong thành phố.
lines: And joining me now is Dana Kowalski from the council's transport team, who's here to talk us through the changes to the Pedal Point bike scheme. Dana, over to you.
Thanks. So, the scheme's been running for six years now, and, well, it's fair to say it's been showing its age.
People often assume the big problem was theft, and yes, we lose a few bikes, but honestly that's never been more than a minor irritation.

The real headache has been distribution. Every weekday morning, the stations in the centre fill up by half past eight and the ones out in the suburbs are bare, and then the whole thing flips in the evening.
Our vans simply can't move bikes around fast enough.
So that, more than anything, is what this overhaul is designed to fix. Now, the change most people will notice first is the e-bikes. We're adding three hundred of them from March.
There was a proposal to let everyone ride them for free for the first month, just to get people hooked, I suppose.
We looked at it hard, but the numbers didn't add up. What we've gone with instead is charging for e-bikes by the minute rather than a flat fee per ride.
So a short hop costs very little, but nobody's tempted to hang on to one all afternoon while it sits outside a café.

Now, some docking stations will be closing, which I know won't be popular with everyone. There was a lot of talk about removing the ones on steep hills, since nobody wants to push a bike up Castle Brow.

But with e-bikes, hills become much less of an issue, so those are staying. The ones going are the stations that see barely a handful of users a day. We'll put that money into bigger stations where demand actually is.
What about people who've already paid for an annual pass? The price for new members goes up to £85 in April.
If you're an existing member, though, you'll keep paying the old rate, and that holds until your current pass comes up for renewal. After that, it's the new price, I'm afraid.
We did consider refunding the difference to people who'd signed up recently, but, frankly, the admin would've cost more than the refunds.
The app's had a complete rebuild, too. I'll be honest, the old one was, um, not much loved.
The live map showing how many bikes are at each station isn't new, it's been there from day one, but it'll now update every thirty seconds instead of every five minutes.
What's genuinely new is that you can hold a bike for up to fifteen minutes before you get to the station, so you're not walking there only to find someone's beaten you to it.
And if you find a bike with a flat tyre or dodgy brakes, you can now flag it straight from the app with a photo, rather than ringing our helpline.
That means the bike gets locked out of use until a mechanic's had a look at it.
People have been asking for a route planner that avoids hills, and group bookings for families. Both are on the list, but realistically, not before next year.
Then there's pricing. The student discount stays exactly as it is, so nothing changes there. But two groups who've never qualified before will now get half-price annual passes.

First, anyone receiving unemployment support, because we know that getting to interviews can be a real expense. And second, night-shift workers at the city's hospitals, who often finish when there are no buses running at all.
We did look at extending the discount to everyone over sixty-five, but they already travel free on the buses, so the case was weaker.
One more thing which has caused a bit of a stir. From May, bikes can't be docked or unlocked in the old town between ten at night and six in the morning.
Some residents had complained about noise, and I understand that, but that's not actually what drove the decision.

The streets there are very narrow and poorly lit, and we've had a worrying number of near misses between bikes and people on foot after dark. Keeping riders out at those hours is about protecting pedestrians, plain and simple.
And finally, we'll be adding around twenty new stations later in the year, and we want local people to tell us where.
We're not running public meetings this time, attendance was dismal last round. Instead, there's an interactive map on the council website where you can drop a pin on the spot you'd like a station.
If enough people pin the same area, it goes on the shortlist. So please, do have a go before the end of February.
Dana Kowalski, thank you very much.

bikes are not in the right places at the right times.

title: Feedback on a dissertation chapter
setting: Hai sinh viên năm cuối và giảng viên hướng dẫn thảo luận nhận xét về chương tổng quan tài liệu trong luận văn của một bạn, chủ đề vì sao người dùng bỏ ứng dụng theo dõi sức khỏe.
lines: Right, Priya, I've gone through your literature review, and Owen's had a read as well, as you asked. Shall we start with the overall shape before we get into the detail?
Please. I'll be honest, I've got a feeling you're going to say it's too long.
Length is the least of it, actually. You're within the limit. What struck me is that it reads as a sequence of summaries. Smith found this, then Jones found that. Each paragraph is one source.
I kind of noticed that too, although I wasn't sure it was a problem. I mean, it was really easy to follow.
Easy to follow, yes. But a reader comes away knowing what each author said, not what the field as a whole thinks, or where it disagrees with itself.
So you'd rather I grouped it by theme. Motivation, design, social features, that kind of thing.
That's the obvious way in, and I think it would serve you well.
Although, couldn't she keep it chronological? The field sort of evolves, doesn't it, from step counters to all the clever stuff now.
It does, but then the story becomes the technology rather than the users. I'm not sure that's the story Priya wants to tell.
No, it isn't. It's about why people give up, not about the gadgets. Themes it is.
OK. What about the number of sources? I was worried I'd leaned too heavily on the older studies.
I wouldn't lose sleep over that. Half the classic work on habit formation is from the nineties, and nobody's overturned it.
I'd go along with Owen there, up to a point. The older work's fine as a foundation. But wearables have changed so much since 2018 that anything on device design really does need to be current.
That's fair. Can we go through the sections one by one? Starting with the definitions section.
Mm. You use 'abandonment', 'disengagement' and 'churn' as if they mean the same thing. Your whole study hinges on that concept, so pin it down. Which one are you measuring?
Abandonment, really. Not opening the app for thirty days.
Thirty days seems a bit arbitrary, though, doesn't it? Why not two weeks?
Because most of the previous studies use thirty, so I can compare like with like.
Then say so, up front, and justify the thirty days.
Can I jump in on the history section? The bit about pedometers in the 1960s. It's interesting, but...
Well, I read it twice and I still couldn't see what it was doing for your argument.
I had a similar reaction, if I'm honest. It's nicely written, but you could lose it and nobody would notice.
Ouch. OK, it goes. What about the section on gamification? I spent ages on that.
And it shows. That's where you actually weigh studies against each other and say which you find more convincing. I'd point to it as a model for the rest of the chapter.
Yeah, I thought that was the best bit by a mile.
That's a relief. And the section on privacy concerns?
You make a strong claim there, that privacy worries are the main reason people quit. That may well be true, but you've got, what, one survey behind it?
Then either find more support or soften the claim. As it stands, an examiner will pounce on it.
Could she not just drop the privacy angle altogether? It's sort of a different dissertation.
No, I'd rather keep it. A lot of my participants actually brought it up.
I'm with Priya on that. It's relevant, it just needs to be better grounded.
OK. Last one, the section on social features, the leaderboards and sharing.
That's solid as a review. But you finish it by describing what your own interviews found. That's results, not literature. It belongs in chapter four.
Oh, I see. I suppose I got carried away.
Happens to all of us. I did exactly the same in my first draft.
So, in terms of priorities, should I restructure first, or deal with the individual sections?
Restructure first. Once it's organised by theme, some of the section-level problems will sort themselves out, and you'll see where the gaps are.
I'd have gone the other way, personally. Fix the small stuff while it's fresh, then reorganise.
You can, but you'll end up rewriting paragraphs twice. I'd really advise against it.
No, that makes sense. Big picture first. And the deadline for the revised version?
Officially the end of the month. But if you can get it to me a week before, I'll have time to give you proper comments rather than a quick skim.
I'll aim for that, then. Thanks, both of you. This has been really useful, even the painful bits.

groups.instr: Questions 21-25. Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

items.q: What does Dr Hallam see as the main problem with the chapter overall?
o: It is difficult for the reader to follow.
items.why: "Length is the least of it... You're within the limit". Vấn đề: "Each paragraph is one source" (tóm tắt từng nguồn riêng lẻ). Owen lại khen là "really easy to follow", nên C sai.

items.q: What is Owen's initial opinion of the chapter's structure?
o: He was uncertain whether it was a weakness.
He thought it should be organised by theme.
He felt it made the chapter too long.
items.why: "I kind of noticed that too, although I wasn't sure it was a problem" = không chắc đó có phải điểm yếu. Ý chia theo chủ đề là của Priya.

items.q: What is Dr Hallam's view of Priya's use of older studies?
o: She should replace most of them with recent research.
They are acceptable for some topics but not others.
They have been contradicted by later work.
items.why: Hallam chỉ đồng ý với Owen "up to a point": nghiên cứu cũ ổn làm nền tảng, nhưng phần về thiết kế thiết bị "really does need to be current" = chấp nhận được với một số chủ đề, không phải tất cả. A sai vì ông không bảo thay phần lớn; C là ý Owen bác bỏ ("nobody's overturned it").

items.q: How does Priya respond to Owen's suggestion about privacy?
o: She rejects it because of her own data.
She says she will discuss it with her participants.
items.why: Owen gợi ý bỏ phần privacy; Priya: "No, I'd rather keep it. A lot of my participants actually brought it up" = từ chối dựa trên dữ liệu của chính mình.

items.q: Why does Dr Hallam want the revised chapter a week early?
o: The official deadline may be brought forward.
He will be away at the end of the month.
He wants to be able to give detailed feedback.
items.why: "I'll have time to give you proper comments rather than a quick skim" = nhận xét chi tiết. Không nhắc đến việc vắng mặt hay đổi hạn.

opts: It needs a clearer focus on one term.
It is the strongest part of the chapter.
Its main claim needs more evidence.
Part of it belongs in another chapter.
It relies too much on one author.

items.why: Priya dùng lẫn "abandonment, disengagement, churn"; Hallam: "pin it down. Which one are you measuring?" = cần làm rõ một thuật ngữ.

items.q: history of pedometers
items.why: "you could lose it and nobody would notice" và Priya: "OK, it goes" = bỏ đi. Hallam khen "nicely written" nhưng đó là bẫy.

items.why: "I'd point to it as a model for the rest of the chapter" và Owen: "the best bit by a mile". Priya nói mất nhiều thời gian nhưng không ai đề nghị mở rộng (G).

items.why: "you've got, what, one survey behind it?... either find more support or soften the claim" = luận điểm chính cần thêm bằng chứng. Owen gợi ý bỏ (A) nhưng bị bác.

items.q: social features
items.why: "you finish it by describing what your own interviews found. That's results... It belongs in chapter four" = một phần nên chuyển sang chương khác.

title: How deep-sea organisms cope with pressure
setting: Bài giảng sinh học biển về cách sinh vật biển sâu thích nghi với áp suất cực lớn ở cấp độ màng tế bào, protein và cơ thể.
lines: Good morning. Last week we looked at temperature and light in the deep ocean. Today I want to turn to what is, arguably, the most unforgiving variable of all down there, and that's hydrostatic pressure.
Pressure increases by roughly one atmosphere for every ten metres of depth, so at the bottom of the deepest trenches, organisms are living under something like a thousand atmospheres.

Now, a common misconception is that the danger is being crushed. It isn't, at least not for animals without air spaces, because water and tissue are almost incompressible. The real problem is far subtler, and it happens at the molecular level.

The underlying principle is that high pressure favours whatever arrangement of molecules takes up the least volume. Any biological process that involves an increase in volume, even a tiny one, is going to be inhibited.
And it turns out that a great many of life's essential processes do exactly that. So let's look at three levels: membranes, proteins, and finally the body as a whole.

Starting with membranes. The lipid molecules in a cell membrane need to be able to move around fairly freely for the membrane to work, for transporting substances in and out, for example. Pressure squeezes these lipids together and makes the membrane more rigid.
In fact, the effect is very similar to cooling. Every thousand metres of depth has roughly the same stiffening effect as a drop of a couple of degrees in temperature.
And, of course, the deep sea is also cold, so the two effects add up.

The solution is one we also see in organisms adapted to cold. Deep-sea species incorporate more unsaturated fatty acids into their membranes. These have kinks in their chains, which stop the molecules packing tightly together, and that keeps the membrane fluid.

More recent work, notably by a group I'll call the Ferreira lab, suggests that membrane shape, specifically its curvature, matters just as much as fluidity, which is something the textbooks haven't quite caught up with yet.
Right, the second level, proteins. A protein only works if it's folded into the correct shape, and many of them also have to bind to other molecules or assemble into larger structures.

Pressure interferes with all of this, partly because water molecules get forced into the protein's interior and distort its structure. Enzymes from shallow-water fish can lose much of their activity at deep-sea pressures.
There are two broad strategies here. One is to change the protein itself, small substitutions in the amino acid sequence that make it less sensitive. But that's a slow, gene-by-gene business.

The other strategy, and this is the one I find genuinely elegant, is to change the environment inside the cell. Deep-sea fish accumulate a small molecule called TMAO, that's trimethylamine N-oxide, which acts as what's known as a piezolyte, or pressure counteractant.

It's thought to work by organising the surrounding water so that it's less likely to invade the protein, effectively stabilising the folded shape. And crucially, it helps all the proteins at once rather than one at a time.
What's striking is that TMAO levels in fish muscle rise steadily with depth. Fish from the surface have relatively little; fish from seven or eight kilometres down have several times as much.
Incidentally, TMAO is what breaks down into the fishy smell of fish that's past its best.
This has led to quite a provocative hypothesis. As TMAO builds up, the fish's internal fluids become more concentrated than the surrounding seawater.
At around eight thousand, sorry, eight thousand two hundred metres, the model predicts they'd become so concentrated that water would start flooding into the tissues.
To prevent that, the fish would need to get rid of salt, but there's no known mechanism for it.
And, interestingly, no fish has ever been recorded much deeper than about eight thousand three hundred metres, although invertebrates such as amphipods live at the very bottom.

So this may explain why fish have a depth limit. I should say, though, the hypothesis is not universally accepted. Some researchers argue that food supply is the more important factor, and that the evidence so far is largely correlational.

Finally, the whole body. The general rule is that gas is a liability. Many shallow-water fish control their buoyancy with a gas-filled swim bladder, but at depth, maintaining a gas volume against that pressure is extremely costly.
So most deep-sea fish have either reduced the swim bladder or lost it altogether, and they rely instead on lipids, which are less dense than water, stored in the liver or in the tissues.
Bodies also tend to be watery and loosely built. The snailfish that live in trenches have soft, almost gelatinous tissue and their skeletons are only partly hardened.
Their skulls, for instance, have gaps in them. Rigid structure is simply not much of an advantage down there.

And this brings me to a practical problem for researchers. When you haul these animals to the surface, the sudden decompression can damage proteins and membranes, so what you study in the lab may not reflect how the animal really functions.

That's why there's been a push for pressure-retaining samplers, which bring specimens up while keeping them at their original pressure. They're expensive, and frankly temperamental, but they're transforming the field.
Right, next week we'll look at feeding strategies, which is where the food supply argument comes back in.

groups.instr: Questions 31-40. Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

items.q: Key principle: high pressure favours molecular arrangements with the smallest ___
items.why: "high pressure favours whatever arrangement of molecules takes up the least volume". Bẫy: nhiều người sẽ ghi "crushed" nhưng giảng viên nói nguy hiểm thật không phải bị nghiền.

items.q: Membranes: pressure makes them more ___ (similar effect to cooling)
items.why: "Pressure squeezes these lipids together and makes the membrane more rigid". Từ "stiffening" xuất hiện ngay sau nhưng không khớp ngữ pháp sau "more".

items.q: Adaptation: more unsaturated fatty acids, whose ___ prevent tight packing
items.why: "These have kinks in their chains, which stop the molecules packing tightly together". "Chains" là bẫy vì có trong câu nhưng không phải thứ ngăn đóng gói.

items.q: Recent research: membrane ___ may be as important as fluidity
items.why: "membrane shape, specifically its curvature, matters just as much as fluidity".

items.q: Proteins: ___ is forced into the protein, distorting its structure
items.why: "water molecules get forced into the protein's interior and distort its structure".

items.q: Strategy 1: changes to the amino acid ___ (slow process)
items.why: "small substitutions in the amino acid sequence", "a slow, gene-by-gene business".

items.q: Strategy 2: TMAO, which protects all proteins at the same time; concentration in muscle increases with ___
items.why: "TMAO levels in fish muscle rise steadily with depth".

items.q: Hypothesis: below about 8,200 m, fish would need to get rid of ___, but no mechanism for this is known
items.why: "the fish would need to get rid of salt, but there's no known mechanism for it". Bẫy: water là thứ tràn vào mô, không phải thứ cần thải ra; TMAO thì đang được tích lũy.

items.q: Some researchers believe ___ supply better explains the depth limit
items.why: "Some researchers argue that food supply is the more important factor".

items.q: Whole body: buoyancy from ___ instead of a swim bladder
items.why: "they rely instead on lipids, which are less dense than water". Gas/swim bladder là thứ bị bỏ, liver chỉ là nơi dự trữ.
